Mr. Speaker, I have the honour and duty to present a petition signed by residents of Edmonton, Alberta. These petitioners are concerned that the trade agreement negotiated by the Government threatens the political and economic sovereignty of Canada by removing the power of the Canadian Government to effectively control such things as foreign ownership, to develop Canadian energy resources in the best interests of Canadians and to equalize opportunities between the regions.
Therefore, these petitioners pray and call upon Parliament to dissolve and allow the people of Canada to accept or reject the proposed free trade agreement.

Mr. Speaker, I also have the honour and duty to present petitions from 100 residents of Whitehorse, Yukon, Iqaluit, Northwest Territories, and Mississauga, Ontario.
These petitioners wish to register their objection to the proposed plutonium flights over the Canadian North, recognizing the potential devastating environmental and nuclear proliferation risks.
Therefore, these petitioners pray and call upon the Parliament of Canada to recognize the danger of such flights and to say no to the transport of plutonium over northern Canadian territory.

speechtext:
The House resumed from Friday, January 29, consideration of the motion of Mr. Bouchard:
That a message be sent to the Senate to acquaint Their Honours that this House agrees with amendments 8 and 13(e) made by the Senate to Bill C-84, an Act to amend the Immigration Act, 1976 and the Criminal Code in consequence thereof, but disagrees with amendments 4, 5(a), (b) and (c), 6(a) and (b), 9, 10, 11, 12 and 13(a) because this House believes they contradict the principles of the Bill for the following reasons:
Amendment 4 would exclude only criminals and war criminals from the refugee determination process, but would allow terrorists, spies and subversives to pursue a claim to refugee status, notwithstanding the fact that Article 33 of the UN Convention would permit the removal of these latter individuals to their countries of nationality or permanent residence, even if they were determined to be Convention refugees.
Amendment 5(a) would eliminate the authority of the Minister to direct a ship to leave or not to enter Canadian waters. This amendment would reopen a significant gap in Canada's ability to control its borders.
Amendments 5(b) and (c) arise out of Senate amendment 5(a), which is not acceptable, and are therefore inappropriate.
Amendments 6(a) and (b) would reverse the policy on which the Immigration Act, 1976 was based, which policy was not changed in the Bill as passed by this House. The amendments jeopardize the possibility of successfully prosecuting persons who profit from organizing illegal migration and from counselling fraud among refugee claimants.
Amendments 9 and 10 would restrict the ability of peace officers and immigration officers to act quickly to search for evidence of major offences under the Immigration Act, 1976, in exigent circumstances, where lives are at risk or where evidence with respect to those offences may be lost or destroyed.
Amendments 11 and 12 would restrict the ability of peace officers and immigration officers to execute search warrants which have been duly authorized by a justice of the peace, by denying explicit authority to break open containers where it is reasonably believed evidence will be found and by limiting the authority to execute these warrants at night.
Amendment 13(a) would reduce the initial period of detention without review from seven days to forty-eight hours, which would allow insufficient time for the gathering of information to substantiate allegations or to identify the individual, particularly when large groups of undocumented persons arrive at one time.

subtopic: IMMIGRATION ACT, 1976 MEASURE TO AMEND-CONSIDERATION OF SENATE AMENDMENTS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise to speak to this Bill and the amendment because I think it goes to the future direction of the country. I am very saddened to think that the Government did not appreciate some of the amendments unanimously agreed to by the Senate. I say that because they were very much in line with the amendments presented by my Party.
Canada signed a UN convention in order to protect refugees all around the world. This Bill directly contradicts that Convention. The people who have made presentations both to the legislative committee as well as the Senate committee understand what is involved because they have been very much involved with refugees. They understood the purpose of the amendment which suggested that instead of turning boats back

February 1, 1988
Immigration Act, 1976
we would look at securing the people who were on the boats and giving them an adequate opportunity to prove whether or not they were refugees.
With this Bill as it stands, we are right back to the kind of situation that existed in 1939 where, to our disgrace, we turned a boatload of Jewish refugees back to Europe at a time when they were being so badly persecuted. The result was that many of them ended up in concentration camps where they were killed. That is the kind of thing we are leaving ourselves open to now if we do not amend this legislation. Certainly there have been judges right across this country, and around the world, who have looked at this Bill and are very concerned at the direction Canada is taking.
We have always been well respected in the international arena and people have felt that Canada was a place that dealt with some sense of fairness and compassion with those who had no place to go. Certainly since we signed the convention 20 years ago we have tried to respect it. Sometimes not as much as we could, but this Bill ensures that we will be seen as not having been sincere in the first place. Certainly the Bill does not respect the Convention.
1 am also concerned about the fact we have not listened to those who have worked very intensively across this country, the church groups and others, and who have said how important it is to make sure of the security and safety of people's lives. We are now just ignoring all of that.
When I looked at the proceedings of the Senate committee it was interesting to see that many of the people who made presentations there had also made presentations to the legislative committee. It seems to me that there is a consistent feeling in the country about this issue and people are taking every opportunity to make the Government sensitive to the fact that this Bill takes us in a direction we have never gone before and one we do not choose to take.
It is important that we recognize that the western world is taking a minimum number of refugees in comparison to the total, and Canada is now saying that it is going to take less than that. We are going to be very selective. We are not going to worry about the fact that people have had to flee without proper documentation. We are not going to worry about that; unless they are properly documented they cannot get in here. It really does not make any sense at all.
There are people who have worked as volunteers at great risk to themselves in order to help those who have escaped to our country in fear of their lives. What we are saying now in this Bill is that those people who are reaching out a hand of compassion are now liable to become criminals in their own country. That certainly does not make any sense. We know that the situation in the world has not eased. The refugee situation has worsened. There are very sensitive areas from which people are fleeing. Some have been taken out of their beds and from their homes in the middle of the night. Some of their families have been able to escape across borders and been
able to reach Canada. We are now saying that those people are not entitled to an adequate hearing.
The United Nations and many groups within Canada are recommending a process for refugee determination and an efficient appeal process. That would allow people to be designated. If we are concerned about safety and security with regard to certain people coming into the country we have the ability of deportation. We are also able to take the time to find them safe refuge in another country before deporting them. I refer to countries such as Chile. We know that if we send people back to that country their lives will be at risk. In taking that attitude toward other people's lives we are being very crass. We are saying that unless they can go through the bureaucratic procedures they will have no refuge in Canada. It does not matter whether they are fleeing for their safety or have no access to any other refuge. This is a disgrace and will be a blot on our history.
I am very surprised that the Government is recommending such legislation because it was very critical when we actually turned a boat around in 1979. The ability to do that exists again. We do not want that kind of thing to happen. We want to keep our reputation in the international community as a caring country. Many of the people who came here after the Hungarian chaos in the 1950s became good citizens of Canada. They built a base in our communities and gave their loyalty to Canada. They realize that if Canada had not accepted them as refugees at that time they would not have lived.
This legislation says that refugees who have experienced great chaos in their own countries will no longer be welcome here. They will not be given time to seek out adequate legal counsel. We are closing doors to people who have not had the opportunity to get the proper documentation. We are saying that refugees who have crossed other borders with false documentation cannot be designated. That is not the kind of thing we want to do.
I am very concerned that in addition to attacking people who could come to this country we are attacking Canadians who, through their generosity and voluntarism, are helping these people. We are telling church groups, community groups, and families whose relatives want to come to this country that if they are helping these people to get through so that they can be identified, they are part and parcel of the problem and can be criminally charged. That is totally unacceptable.
Many of the amendments proposed by the Senate are part and parcel of the amendments which our Party recommended. It was very interesting that all the groups which made presentations suggested the same kinds of amendments. There is no doubt in my mind that the immigration laws were in chaos and the whole procedure had to be streamlined. We needed designation of refugees and designation of immigrants rather than having them all part and parcel of the same pool
February 1, 1988

with regard to numbers and quotas. We need people with expertise in refugee designation.
It would not take much longer than six months to go through that process in a humane, fair, and just way. Instead, we are bringing in a very restrictive Bill which will stop people from being designated. We will be sending them back, probably to their deaths in many cases, because they do not conform to our terms of reference for admittance to this country.
Surely a country like Canada, with so many resources and so much freedom, should be the first to give people a fair hearing and ensure that we provide a safe haven for any refugee whose life is in danger. Anyone who comes to our borders and claims refugee status should be given a hearing and an opportunity to compile their case. They should be entitled to a fair and honest appeal process. With the legislation before us we are telling the volunteers and church groups right across the country that we will have none of that. We will tighten the immigration laws to the extent that we will be so selective as to probably admit to Canada only white people who have half a million dollars.
It is a disgrace to set such criteria for admittance to the country. However, the larger problem will be in the long term. We know that our country is not renewing its population with its own birth rate. We will be admitting into this country people who will be very self-serving and without a sense of a pluristic society.
Up to now we have built a country with a mosaic of which we have all been very proud. The refugees who have sought haven here have made a tremendous commitment to the country and have helped us to understand the international scene and to have compassion because our roots are all so different. I would like to think that because of the mosaic we have in this country we have built a pluristic society which understands the enrichment of different cultures coming together, not in confrontation but in understanding of each other.
The volunteers, community groups, and church groups are recommending that the system be made more efficient but that the doors not be closed. They say that they want our country to continue to be a refuge for people who cannot find a safe refuge anywhere else in the world.
If every country is so restrictive on this issue the problem will become much more serious everywhere. If this legislation is passed it will probably be the most restrictive anywhere in the western world. I am particularly concerned about that because, in addition to putting people's lives in jeopardy, we are losing our international credibility as mediators and peacekeepers in the international field. We are saying that people coming to our shores must be treated in a very legalistic and non-compassionate manner and that if they do not conform to our system they will be turned around.
Immigration Act, 1976
I was most shocked by the fact that we could actually turn boats around at sea. Furthermore, it has been suggested that the Coast Guard be authorized to take this action. The Coast Guard is not trained in immigration policy and is not supposed to decide who can enter our country. The Coast Guard's function is much different from the immigration policy they are being asked to follow now. It does not make any sense that the Government is putting that kind of pressure on those people by delegating that kind of responsibility to them.
We could see the same thing we saw in 1939 when boats were turned back. I do not think there is anyone in the House who is not embarrassed about or does not regret that action in 1939.
That incident should be a lesson to us to avoid legislation that seems to condone such action.
I hope the Government seriously considers that this legislation is restrictive. It is not a coincidence that many of the same groups have appeared before both the parliamentary committee and the Senate committee, at a great cost to themselves. The Senate committee was unanimous in its amendments. The Government should get the message that this legislation is unacceptable to Canadians. The more that Canadians learn about this legislation the less acceptable it becomes.
On behalf of Canadians now and Canadians in the future, I plead with the Government to withdraw this legislation which could become a scar on our history. We want to have a proud history that shows that we honour and take responsibly the conventions we sign. This legislation does not do that, and it must be opposed. If the Government is unwilling to accept the amendments it should withdraw the legislation.

subtopic: IMMIGRATION ACT, 1976 MEASURE TO AMEND-CONSIDERATION OF SENATE AMENDMENTS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I welcome the opportunity this morning to take part in the debate on Bill C-84. Immigration policy has always been a priority for the Liberal Party. The Liberal Government left a very solid foundation, and thanks to this legacy, the Conservative Government has been able to maintain and enhance our prestige on the international scene. However, Mr. Speaker, 1 find it hard to understand some of the measures being proposed in this Bill. In any event, I want to start by considering the immigration issue, first in terms of the world situation and second, in terms of the role Canada has to play.
The world situation. For over two centuries, people on this planet have been seeking independance and throwing off the bonds of their oppressors, thus becoming sovereign. We saw this phenomenon in Europe during the nineteenth century. At the time, the industrial revolution was accompanied by a number of popular uprisings. The monarchy, the Czars and other forms of government gave way to governments with a popular base, in many cases democratic governments. We have all read about the French Revolution, the popular uprising in

February 1, 1988
Immigration Act, 1976
Germany, the painful transition from monarchy to parliamentary system in England, and, even closer to home, the American Revolution next door. All these events produced a host of refugees trying to escape oppression in their native countries. At the time, many newly liberated European countries wanted colonies in order to expand their markets and sources of raw materials. Thus, England founded its empire, as did France, Holland, Spain and Germany. Many of the colonies were located in Africa and Asia. Subsequently, these new colonies also wanted to manage their own destiny and become the sovereign nations they were entitled to be. We remember the Congo, Algeria, and more recently Mozambique, all of which wanted their freedom as a nation. They achieved their freedom at great cost, and, as in the nineteenth century, the process was sometimes very violent. Every time, a stream of refugees was the result.
There are two other major upheavals that disrupted this planet, and I am referring to the two Great Wars. We all remember that these wars produced a large number of refugees. Not long ago, we saw many refugees arriving in Canada from Vietnam, Cambodia and Laos, and today, we all are very much aware of the situation of Blacks in South Africa and their experience of the violence of a discriminatory regime.
We are priviledged to live in country like Canada where peace prevails in a democratic system. That is not the case on the international scene. It is a jungle where each country tries to get what it can. The United Nations contains the seed of an international political system. Until the people of this earth reach a common agreement, based on co-operation and good will, and take action accordingly, nations will continue to violate the basic principles of human rights, and refugees will roam this planet, seeking a safe haven from the pain and suffering to which they have been subjected.
One country that is an oasis for all these refugees, is, as you may have guessed, Mr. Speaker, Canada. The Liberal Party led the way in this respect, under the leadership of Louis St-Laurent, Lester Pearson and Pierre Trudeau. Unfortunately, with Bill C-84 we may be sending the wrong signals to the international community. What the Conservative Government is about to do with Bill C-84 is exactly that. We know, for instance, that it is very difficult for people living in Central America to enter the United States.
I wish Government Members would understand that we agree there is abuse in the system and that we should deal with the problem. However, the Government's aggressive approach has blown out of all proportion a problem that could have been dealt with quite simply. Earlier, I talked about what causes the refugee phenomenon, and I did so to explain why any action taken by Canada must be seen within a broader context. When we focus on very narrow issue of refugees who abuse the system in Canada, we tend to forget the problem is much broader and far more complex. Canada has often been very generous in assisting people in difficulty throughout the world.
I am thinking, for instance, of the plight of Ethiopia. Our aid has made it possible for many Ethiopians to stay in their
country. Our approach internationally should be a preventive one. We should work on eliminating the situations that generate refugees. In fact, this perspective is entirely in the Liberal tradition which has always encouraged aid, peace making and mediation.
So far, a lot has been said about Bill C-84, but very little about the persons concerned by this Bill. Who are these refugees? I will give an example of a family I happen to know. This family was living in Chile at the time of the 1970 coup. The police came to their home and knocked on the door. The wife had time to take her two little girls and run to the back of the house. The policemen came in through the front door and took the husband, a university professor. His wife and their two children barely had time to escape through the back door.
[DOT] (N40)
The husband was executed. His wife fled to Canada with the children. They arrived without papers, still dazed, and then had to cope with adjusting to a new country, new customs, a new language, the children without their father, the wife without her husband.
There are hundred of stories like that. There is an Indian saying: To understand another person, one has to walk a mile in his moccasins. In other words, one has to put oneself in the other person's place.
I suggest Hon. Members put themselves in the place of the refugees who enter this country and are faced with the new measures proposed by this Government in Bill C-84. Imagine a family that just crossed the Atlantic and faces a Coast Guard officer who has to decide whether they are genuine refugees. Imagine a refugee who is unfairly denied refugee status and cannot appeal the decision. Would you want to be treated like that?
If you were sent back to your own country, to certain death, what would your reaction be?
My colleagues have given all kind of reasons why Bill C-84 is unsatisfactory. I wonder what the present Government's real objectives are. In 1974, we had 200,000 immigrants. In 1986, we had only 87,000. In addition, the number of family-class immigrants dwindled from 51,981 to 12,798 between 1984 and 1986-10,000 fewer. This Bill was introduced after 300-odd people landed on our shores. As underscored by my colleague from York West (Mr. Marchi), over the two years when the boat people came here Canada became home to 106,000 individuals. I must therefore conclude that the Conservative Government has locked the immigration door and has no intention of welcoming immigrants: it is making a federal case out of 300 people arriving here, whereas a Liberal Government did let in 106,000 immigrants in 1979 and 1980.
The message sent out by the Conservative Government has already registered. In her release dated August 17, 1980, CLC President Shirley Carr noted that "during a recent tour of Central America CTC representatives were approached on a
February 1, 1988

number of occasions by labour union supporters who expressed dismay over the fact that Canada seems to be discarding the humanitarian principles to which it had subscribed for years and years".
Like my Liberal colleagues, I believe this Bill eliminates the right of appeal, it is contrary to the spirit of the United Nations covenant and, first and foremost, treats churches and humanitarian institutions like criminals.
Religious organizations do not want to find themselves on the wrong side of the law. Such organizations made it possible for that Chilean woman and the two children to escape from their country.
Do my Conservative Party colleagues really think that a person fleeing under death threats can walk in a Canadian consulate or tell the nearest police officer: "Just a minute, 1 want to leave the country, let me get a Canadian visa". No way, we must remember that her husband was killed to realize the futility of such a gesture.
With this legislation the Conservative Government wants to close one of the very few ways open to these refugees, namely religious institutions and organizations.
Do Conservatives Members fail to see that people working for religious organizations have a law which is much more basic than any civil law or any government law? The law of these religious organizations, their belief in a superior being, is infinitely fairer than any human legislation. Their conscience tells them to disobey civil laws if these laws show no respect for human decency.
The Senate amendment would help clear up that situation. As a matter of fact I fail to understand the logic of the Conservative Government. It shirks its responsibilities and lets churches come to the assistance of the most destitute people in our society. In 1987, the International Year of Shelter for the Homeless, some religious organizations went to the rescue of homeless in Canada. What this Tory Government is saying is that since there is a shelter problem for the homeless, let charitable organizations take care of it. But with this legislation, it is saying to them: Do not take care of the shelter problem of the homeless elsewhere in the world. It is illegal. The Government of Canada is now deciding what is charitable and what is not.
Let us make no mistake about it: Refugees are people who are both without home and without country. Where is Canada when the time comes to stand up and be counted? During the International Year of Shelter for the Homeless, we organized a world conference. We spent money for all sorts of conferences, studies, projects. Bill C-84 clearly demonstrates that this Government is involved in a window-dressing job, a PR campaign, and that it does not understand anything of the problems the homeless are facing both here and elsewhere in the world. What is in store for religious organizations are jail terms when, for the same charitable purposes, they try to help citizens of the world who are seeking an oasis of peace.
Immigration Act, 1976
1 suggest that, seen from this angle, the Senate's amendment should be fully reconsidered or altered to take into account the positive and necessary contributions of religious and charitable organizations in this context. This brings me to deal with the relevancy of the Senate's amendment concerning the forcing back of boats.
I am concerned about the Government's refusal of this amendment for two reasons. First of all, the passengers of such a boat would be denied any recourse, which is a blatant violation of our judiciary system. Also, and as a consequence, what the Tory Government is saying is: Not in my backyard! In other words, we do not want this problem in Canada. That is where Canada is missing the boat. Not only would this approach not prevent smugglers from continuing their trade, as the Official Opposition critic explained, but Canada would be sending a very clear message to the international community: Don't count on Canada any more. Is that the price Canada must pay to be part of the group of industrialized nations, the Group of Seven? Or is Canada giving up its role as a world leader in this field?
Mr. Speaker, the Government is always saying we should be opening up new markets by being competitive and developing our technology. That is how a nation is measured, but there are other ways as well. Canada has always been a leader in immigration. In fact, Canada was the world leader. Why is the Conservative Government trying to downgrade this country to the level of other countries that are economically well off but fail miserably in terms of their immigration policies and the way they treat other people on this planet?
I therefore urge the Government to adopt the Senate's amendment concerning the provision for turning back ships, or to at least amend it so that refugees will have legal recourse.
Canada's message to other nations must be clear: "The buck stops here".
We will not let refugees be literally shipped from country to country without giving them some legal recourse. We will not accept a replay of the kind of situation we saw during World War II, when a ship with Jewish refugees was refused entry by Canada and several other coutries.
The Hon. Member for York West (Mr. Marchi) mentioned in the House the provisions of this Bill that will probably be considered to be unconstitutional.
Considering last week's historic decision on abortion by the Supreme Court I suggest that the Government make sure its Bill is indeed constitutional.
In concluding, I would like to make it clear that we, as Liberals, agree that any abuse of our system must be dealt with, but we do not agree this means destroying the whole system.
I may add that we, as Canadians, are privileged among the nations of this world, and that we have a duty to keep our doors and our minds open to the less fortunate on this planet.

February 1, 1988
Immigration Act, 1976
If we look at the context of this problem and the long-term implications, the sight of 300 people arriving in Canada should not make us panic. I think that the suggestion by the Hon. Member for York West that Canadians should be informed of the many benefits that accrue to Canada as a result of immigration is a very positive one, in keeping with the best traditions of this House. The Hon. Member is to be commended!
Finally, Canada must continue to play a leading role in the world, co-operating with other countries in the search for a solution that respects human dignity.
The Senate's amendments and those suggested by the Hon. Member for York West are a step in that direction. 1 urge the Government to revise its decision and to accept those amendments.

We are not really debating the legislation; we are debating suggested amendments made by the Senate.
The Minister has outlined for the benefit of the House the considerable difficulties that would be created in terms of our capacity to protect ourselves as a nation from terrorists, from criminals and from undesirable people if some of the Senate amendments were accepted. The purpose in returning to the House last summer was to bring forward this piece of legislation. It received careful consideration in committee. It certainly received careful consideration in the Senate. We are now in a filibuster situation in the House of Commons.
As a Calgarian, I am very aware that in some two weeks we will be into the Olympic Games in Calgary. Historically, the Olympics have experienced some unfortunate terrorist incidents. In the City of Toronto in the not too distant future world leaders will meet. These leaders are potential targets for terrorists.
As a result of benign neglect over many years Canada was left in an essentially defenseless position in terms of immigration law. We are trying to correct that. A minority of Members in the House through their behaviour and through the continuation of this debate are simply denying the majority of Members the opportunity to vote on whether or not the Minister has brought forward a reasonable response to the
amendments of the Senate. There is still an urgent situation in the country to correct the situation.
I say to the Hon. Member that not only have I studied these matters over the last two or three years as Chairman of the committee, but during the hearings that were held daily we went into great detail about this situation. There was also a clause-by-clause study of the Bill in committee. Subsequently, I spent a week in Geneva at an executive council meeting of the United Nations High Commissioner for Refugees. A great deal of my time there was spent with the legal experts of the High Commissioner's office who went over in some detail both Bill C-84 and Bill C-55, as amended. I point out to Hon. Members that what is before the House are not the original pieces of legislation but the amended versions.
I came away from there able to say on public platforms across the country that no one was able to bring to my attention the specific legislation of any country which provided more legal protection for true refugees than would be true in Canada once these amended Bills are passed. With our present procedures in place we do not have something to which the rest of the world can look to Canada as an example. These procedures are archaic and difficult. They cause a great deal of unnecessary and unwanted publicity for true refugees. I say that because people abuse bad law. We have bad law in place today and it is being abused.
What we brought forward to the House and what committees have worked very hard on is the creation of good law to which the rest of the world can look to. I simply ask the Hon. Member, if she feels that this piece of legislation is really so rotten, can she provide to the House the name of a single country anywhere in the world which will provide better protection to true refugees than will be true of the combination of Bill C-84 and Bill C-55?
Not only is the legislation which is before us not bad, it will be the finest legislation that exists in the world in terms of providing legal protection to refugees. I defy anyone in the House to stand up and give an example of one country that will do the job better than Canada will do it once this filibuster is over. It is time for the House to vote on this matter.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is not so much of a question, but more of a statement in response to some of the allegations made by the Parliamentary Secretary. He likes to suggest that thoughtful, positive debate is a filibuster. I wish to remind the Parliamentary Secretary that the Government may have the largest majority in Canadian history, but that does not mean that it can run roughshod over Parliament.
Parliament was recalled during the summer to pass this Bill expeditiously. The Government felt that it could ignore the advice of all of the people who have expertise in this area, come in with a Draconian piece of legislation, and use its huge majority to jam it through the House of Commons. Thank goodness, in our parliamentary system that does not work. To a certain extent, there are checks and balances.
While I have personal views that are not necessarily positive about the other place, the fact that the Minister of Employment and Immigration (Mr. Bouchard) has agreed to make some changes to the legislation is proof enough that it was erred or seriously flawed. Because we are trying to propose ways and means of improving this legislation as responsible members of opposition Parties, the suggestion that this is a filibuster, I find unacceptable.
I remember Canada in 1979 pleading heavily with countries in Southeast Asia to accept the boat people as they were fleeing persecution. Canada was urging countries to be compassionate, to be humanitarian, and to provide a safe

February 1, 1988
Immigration Act, 1976
haven for those people who were fleeing what they perceived to be a very negative environment in their home country.
If someone feels that a ship approaching Canada is filled with illegal refugees, this legislation states that we will use our navy or our Coast Guard to force the boat to turn around and return to its port of origin. How on earth will anyone determine whether or not there are legitimate refugees on board? This is obviously a silly provision. I wish to remind my friend, the Parliamentary Secretary, that there have only been two cases in Canadian history where refugees have arrived by boat. This is simply one example, and there are many others, where my friends in opposition are attempting to explain to the Government that changes must be made to make this a reasonable and acceptable piece of legislation. 1 find it completely unacceptable that our responsible debates are called a filibuster.

subtopic: IMMIGRATION ACT, 1976 MEASURE TO AMEND-CONSIDERATION OF SENATE AMENDMENTS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am glad to have the opportunity to participate in this debate and present the views of my Party on Bill C-84 and the amendments that the Senate has proposed to it.
It seems obvious to me, and I think it must now be obvious to the Canadian people, that this whole issue and this whole legislation was phoney from the start. The Government never did have a reasonably founded apprehension that there would be large numbers of refugees arriving in Canada by boat. There never was any degree of reasonable apprehension that among those refugees there would be terrorists or criminals. There never was any evidence presented to Parliament or to any other forum to suggest that the recall of Parliament in August, 1986, was necessary. We had a phoney recall. We have a phoney Bill. We have a phoney problem based on a phoney analysis, and what I believe is a false apprehension.
One has to wonder if in fact this was done in order to help the failing election campaign of the Ontario Progressive Conservatives under their then Leader, Larry Grossman. If so, obviously it misfired.
This country won the Nansen Medal for its treatment of refugees over a period of some 20 years. The Government decided to tear up that record and that reputation in an attempt to generate some positive response from the voting public by undertaking a campaign that had as its targets those who were in the weakest position to defend themselves.
It has been argued, and argued by many authorities, that the provisions of Bill C-84 as originally proposed violate the Charter of Rights and Freedoms. It has also been argued that its provisions violate the United Nations Convention on the treatment of refugees.
Many organizations have been critical of the Bill, and I should like to start by exploring one of the points which the Parliamentary Secretary was attempting to make. The obvious point of the Bill is to take action against Central American
refugees and those who come here by water. They are the easiest to identify or to pick out. They generally have the least in the way of available resources to assist them in making a refugee claim.
The Parliamentary Secretary spoke of 750 to 800 persons per months arriving and making refugee claims. He knows that the majority of those people in fact have proper identification and that the majority of those people come from such countries as Brazil, Portugal, and Turkey. Normally they are in possession of, at least when they board the aircraft, purportedly proper identification in the form of passports or visas. What happens in the case of those people is that sometimes they get through. Sometimes the deception is detected, and then they go on an individual basis through the refugee determination process.
The very idea that a criminal, unless a highly unsuccessful one, a terrorist or someone who is a security risk to Canada would choose to arrive by the slowest, the riskiest, and the leakiest means possible, for example, a tramp steamer trying to sneak in under cover of fog to a coast that is in many ways hazardous to impromptu landings, is risible. For the Government to suggest by way of the Bill that that sort of landing constitutes a threat to Canada's security is frankly a deception.
Many criticism were levelled against Bill C-84 when it was first introduced. I think it is worth while repeating them. People who are the subject of a security certificate will be removed from Canada without the legal right to make a refugee claim. Another criticism was that turning boats around permits the operator to escape without a penalty. The boat could return however many times and be turned around. Obviously the sanctions proposed against groups who assist refugee claimants are unacceptable since many of them could come under the threat of such sanctions through inadvertence.
Only a few years ago we were encouraging the countries of southeast Asia to take in boat people who, obviously in the degree of desperation that led them to get on those boats, were refugees. We put passengers on those boats at risk if we simply turn the boat around at sea. We put them at the risk of the master of the vessel deciding to make some riskier approach or deciding to wreck the ship so that it cannot be turned around, whatever the risk to the passengers. We have no way, in such a case, of finding out who the people are, where they are coming from, what their reasons are, or whether in fact they are second-hand refugees, those who have been driven to desperation by the poor treatment they received in their original country of lodging outside their home country.
If people are dumped into the sea because a captain has not taken them back to the point of embarkation, apparently the Bill makes it an offence for a passing ship to pick them up. The Security Intelligence Review Committee is already overloaded. Also, the retention provisions are unnecessary and violate the Charter of Rights and Freedoms. The rejection rate for refugee claimants has historically averaged from 65 per cent to
February 1, 1988

70 per cent, which is something we should bear in mind in considering the Bill.
With regard to the Senate amendments 1 could go on-and undoubtedly I will at a future opportunity-at some length about the legitimacy of the Senate and the legitimacy of Senate adjustments or amendments to Bills which go to the Senate Chamber. However, this is not the time or the place to question, as I certainly would, the legitimacy of the Senate. The fact is that the Senate has produced some reasonable amendments which address many of the major objections to the Bill. I must say also that the Government has had the sense in some instances to accept amendments which are worth while and frankly to take away some, though certainly not all, of the objectionable aspects of the legislation.
I do not think that some of the original stated objections of the Government in the Bill are such that many would object to them. It is clearly necessary to place an increased responsibility on transportation companies to know who they are transporting and to know exactly under what status or claim the person is boarding a vessel or airplane in order to come to Canada. I do not think that is something we find objectionable. It does not go contrary to Canadian traditions as does much of the legislation.
1 am glad to see, for example, the Government accepting the Senate amendment which would permit a person who is the subject of a security certificate to be present during the presentation of the Government's case to the judge except where there are compelling reasons for exclusion. In today's environment of international terrorist activity against some states and institutions, I suppose we can conceive of a situation where a person's very appearance before the judge would have some risk to Canadians. It is not easy to do so, but nevertheless it is a possibility. Therefore, the acceptance of this amendment with the inherent flexibility for situations of extreme danger or urgency is at last something intelligent from the Government.
However, the Senate amendment which would remove the power to order a ship not to enter or to leave Canadian waters has been rejected by the Government. I can only see that as being a mistake. As I see it, the effect is that if Canada is able to communicate with a vessel that is within range of Canadian shores to make purportedly an attempt to land refugees, surely with the technology available or at the disposal of our Armed Forces and Coast Guard we have the obvious opportunity to apprehend the vessel at the very instant it enters Canadian waters or beaches on Canadian soil. Surely it is much better that we should know who is trying to enter Canada and why than that we should simply cast them adrift on the high sea, a practice which used to be known as marooning and of course implies the possibility of very high mortality among the victims.
Earlier 1 mentioned Canada's recent history because the two cases before this decade of ships full of refugees being turned away from Canadian shores are dark stains on the country's tradition of magnanimity and generosity to refugees. In recent
Immigration Act, 1976
history Canada has had a very good record in the treatment of refugees and of refugee claimants. That is a record which we should be seeking to sustain. Let us see if we can earn the Nansen Medal again sometime.
In terms of the measures in the Bill, which I for one do not find objectionable, the action to increase penalties on those who smuggle people into Canada or across borders for profit or gain is a very necessary control. However, characteristically the Government has lumped them together in Bill C-84 with measures which neither I nor my Party can support. Obviously preventing the entry of terrorists or criminals is a legitimate and worthy government objective. What we are saying about Bill C-84 is that it will have its hardest impact on those who are neither terrorists nor criminals.
In recent months, we have heard that the Government is seeking a safe third country for people who are turned away from Canadian shores. What does that tell us about what we have learned? I received a letter from a resident of Dollard des Ormeaux in Quebec who concludes by saying:
I remember learning in school about how Canada turned away boatloads of
Jews. Haven't we learned from the past?
Of course, those people did not go to a safe third country, they went back to a very dangerous situation indeed.
An example of comment in the press is that in recent years, Canada has been the most generous of western countries with regard to refugees and we have been congratulating ourselves endlessly about this. Perhaps we have, though it does bear repeating. It also bears repeating that not every person who comes claiming to be a refugee should be accepted as a refugee. Again, my belief is that before the advent of Bill C-84, we had adequate means to determine that.
We are after all largely a country, if not of refugees then certainly of refugees and immigrants. It is even stated by some ethnographers and historians that the aboriginal people of this country came to North America some 30,000 years ago via an ice bridge. That, of course, is now something that is beyond a reasonable determination, but apart from the aboriginal people of Canada, it is absolutely certain that all who have come here since, their descendants and those who will continue to come to Canada in the future, are immigrants all and in some cases refugees.
In the past, Canada's golden years of immigration included 1910 when over 400,000 people came largely from eastern Europe to settle the Canadian Prairies. We must truly recognize the contribution refugees have made to building the Canada we have, love and enjoy today.
There has to be a better way for the Government to get a judgment on the constitutionality of a piece of legislation than to submit it to Parliament and leave it to its fate before the courts. It has been said that a problem with Bill C-84 is that it may eventually be found unconstitutional, and 1 am sure there

February 1, 1988
Immigration Act, 1976
are lessons for all of us in last week's Supreme Court judgment as to what happens in such a case.
We are glad to see the Liberal Party now on side so far as Bill C-84 is concerned. We noted, of course, the comments in The Ottawa Citizen of July 18 of last year made by the Leader of the Liberal Party (Mr. Turner), but we are glad to see that the Liberal Party is also debating this measure with us in the House of Commons.

subtopic: IMMIGRATION ACT, 1976 MEASURE TO AMEND-CONSIDERATION OF SENATE AMENDMENTS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I think the Hon. Member will realize that this Bill passed the House some months ago and was in the Senate for a very long time. When it was considered by the Senate, amendments were made and then some of those amendments were accepted by the Government in an effort to put the Bill through. Now the Bill is back in the House with a Senate position that is not reasonable. The Hon. Member's Party continues to speak about the Bill. Surely a Government is entitled to get its legislation through in a six-month, eight-month or nine-month period. The continual discussion and support of the Senate by the New Democratic Party is really something to behold.
My question to the Hon. Member deals with whether it is his view and his Party's view that those who conspire to break Canada's immigration laws should somehow be relieved of real search-and-seizure proceedings and should now be entitled to be treated as other than offenders. This is bearing in mind that there has been all sorts of evidence of people paying $3,000
$4,000 and $5,000 and even up to $10,000 for phoney documentation that would allow them to get onto planes, and for the organization of phoney immigration by way of refugee claims into Canada. Is it not his Party's view that that kind of thing that tears apart Canadian sovereignty ought to be a crime and that people who commit that kind of crime ought to be subject to the full penalties set out in Bill C-84?

subtopic: IMMIGRATION ACT, 1976 MEASURE TO AMEND-CONSIDERATION OF SENATE AMENDMENTS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would like to thank the Hon. Member for his question, though the strawmen were falling with such speed during it that I had difficulty counting them as they went down.
The Hon. Member must surely have heard me compliment the Government on its reasonableness in accepting some of the Senate amendments. As far as the time taken to get the Bill through the Senate is concerned, I would contend, and I think anyone who looked at the record would support me, that the time taken in the Senate was a reflection of the fact that the Government chose not to try to use any degree of powerful influence on the Senate to get this through faster. Certainly that indicates that the Government's effort to get this through the Senate was not up to the emergency billing the Government gave this measure when it recalled Parliament.
As far as phoney claims are concerned, I would repeat the point I made earlier in my speech. The Hon. Member talks of conspiracy. He talks of thousands of dollars changing hands for false documentation. No one disputes that this happens. We are saying, however, that Bill C-84 is only tangentially related to that sort of thing.
The fact is that it is an absolute sophistry to say that 150 or 180 people on a boat were conspiring to break Canadian immigration laws. They obviously knew nothing of Canadian immigration laws. Those who do conspire by procuring false documents are indeed knowing offenders, but the fact is that the measures to control that sort of entry into Canada were largely pre-existing.
What we have here basically are measures which would put in jeopardy the very lives of people who are generally too poor, too ignorant and too desperate to even form an intent to conspire against Canada's immigration laws, and who in many cases are not really aware except in the most fuzzy and haphazard way that those laws exist and will be enforced.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the President of the Privy Council
subtopic: IMMIGRATION ACT, 1976 MEASURE TO AMEND-CONSIDERATION OF SENATE AMENDMENTS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the Hon. Member talked about democracy. When his colleagues stand up and chastise the Government for listening to a "goon squad", they are chastising us for listening to Members of Parliament who represent their constituents. The NDP has a rather weird idea of what is involved in a democracy. It seems some of their ideas would be more in accord with a dictatorship.
The Hon. Member mentioned the provisions of this Bill dealing with boats. I would like to let the House know that I think the difference between a filibuster, which is what we are
February 1, 1988

experiencing now for the fifth day, and an informed debate is the degree to which Members are truly informed and they lay information on the table germane to the issue.
In 1985, some two years ago, this Government took a world leadership position to develop a scheme which is referred to in the UN as RASRO, or the Rescue At Sea Resettlement Office. We are a signatory to that agreement. It encourages ship captains to pick up people adrift at sea in leaky boats and give them sanctuary on the ship. The captain is guaranteed that he can come to port and disembark those people. We took the lead in that initiative and we have an obligation under that treaty to resettle our fair share of those kinds of people.
That was concrete action taken by this Government with respect to boat people. What 1 hear the Opposition saying is that as we change Canadian immigration law, we should continue to leave in place provisions which would encourage the peddlers in human flesh to go to these desperate people, take their life savings, and cast them adrift in a leaky boat in the North Atlantic, one of the most hazardous oceans in the world. That is what they want us to do. Or, they would have us encourage those peddlers in human flesh to put those people on a great big leaky boat and take it to our shores, not a port or someplace with wharfs, but past the rocks and shoals and waves which threaten to capsize the boats.
1 say to Hon. Members that if Conservative Members in this House were to give in to the Opposition, that is what we would be doing. We would be encouraging the peddling of human flesh by unscrupulous people and putting the health and safety of these people at risk. Members of this Party say no. You can filibuster all you want but we will do nothing to encourage further traffic in misery. We are trying to stop it.
The Hon. Member says terrorists and criminals have access to expensive suits of clothing, false passports, and so on. There is no evidence that anyone comes in and claims to be a refugee when in fact they are a terrorist, he says. That simply defies reality. Surely the Hon. Those are not all the people who arrived. Those are the ones turned over to the RCMP so we could try to find out who they are. Does he honestly believe that we should leave the law alone so that they can just walk right into the country, 10,000 a year, and we do not know who they are? subtopic: IMMIGRATION ACT, 1976 MEASURE TO AMEND-CONSIDERATION OF SENATE AMENDMENTS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am taking part in this debate because 1 consider that, although there is an urgent need for both our refugee legislation and our Immigration Act to be re-examined and updated, this particular Bill has flaws and needs a lot of work. 1 found it distressing this morning to hear the Parliamentary Secretary, who is normally a thoughtful Member and from whom one would have expected better, dismissing all the genuine concerns on this side of the House as filibustering.
I am going to begin by laying out what is still wrong with the Bill, what could be corrected relatively simply with some good will on the part of the Minister, and then return to some basic principles on which I think we can agree.
First, one must point out that the recommendations of the Senate Committee on Legal and Constitutional Affairs were unanimous. Not only Liberal Senators supported the amendments before us, so did Conservative Senators. In this particular case the chamber of sober second thought did a rather good job.
The Minister, indeed, has admitted that his legislation was born in haste, because he has accepted some of those amendments. He has accepted that claimants may be in courtrooms when lawyers for the Government present a security or criminal intelligence report about them, unless the claimant poses a security or personal safety risk. This is surely an improvement on the original situation where a genuine claimant, who might be represented by a not very well informed or not very competent lawyer, was at risk, not knowing what had been said, and therefore not in a position to counter arguments. The state will still be protected because there is provision to exclude people when there is a clear and known security risk.
As to the question of threat of criminal prosecution against church workers or others who assist refugee claimants, the Minister is now prepared to guarantee that that will not happen without formal consent of the Attorney General of Canada. In other words, the church worker who in good faith

February 1, 1988
Immigration Act, 1976
tries to assist someone to make a refugee claim is now not liable to punishment as was the case with the original Bill.
The amendment which the Minister has refused to entertain and which I seriously urge he re-examine is the one which allows boats to be turned back on the high seas. Apparently the Minister considers that there is some deterrent value in this. Surely, on the contrary, there is an enormous risk in this. If an unscrupulous ship's captain on a leaky, poorly provisioned, and poorly staffed boat on the high seas in the North Atlantic is turned back by our Coast Guard officials, what is the deterrent to him? He takes his unfortunate passengers back and dumps them somewhere or other. He still has their money and so has not lost anything.
Surely a much more effective deterrent would be to bring that ship into port, confiscate it, charge the captain, and jail him if necessary. That would be an effective deterrent but, of at least the same importance, Canadian officials would be able to examine those people on board and determine whether or not they were genuine refugees. If they were turned back on the high seas we would know nothing about them and they could be genuine refugees. That is the reason I think that particular amendment made by the Senate should be regarded seriously. The Minister has turned it down out of hand. I hope he will reconsider because that is an important part of the opposition of my Party to this Bill as it now stands.
This Bill was introduced in great haste in response to the arrival of a boat carrying 150 refugee applicants to Nova Scotia last summer. The Minister has been saying ever since that he needs Draconian powers in order to deal with fake refugees. However, there are powers in the present legislation which are not being used. A lot of the fake refugee applications are coming from unscrupulous so-called immigration consultants and lawyers. Section 95(n) of the present Immigrations Act allows prosecution of those who would counsel or assist illegal immigrants. That section has not been used other than to prosecute the captain of the Amelie.
The most extraordinary abuses are taking place and the Government remains inactive. In my own riding four or five immigration consultants have set up shop. They charge fees for counseling people on making false immigration applications. They have links with travel agents in various countries. The Government knew about this for years before it finally acted. It has finally laid charges against three of them but there is no indication when those cases will be brought to trial.
The first line of protection for us is surely to prosecute the people who are organizing the scams. Many of the people who have made false refugee claims do not know our laws and have paid large sums of money to these consultants who have advised them that this is the way to come into Canada. The key way to stop this must be to deal with these fake immigration consultants and with employers who knowingly hire illegals at poor wages.
There has been for at least two years, to my knowledge, a lively traffic in social insurance cards and the Government is not on top of that. There are some remarkably youthful looking people working in Toronto with cards which show that they are 65. They do not look a day over 21 or 22 but the Government is not acting on that.
Returning to the immigration law itself, I think we would all agree that the law as passed in 1976 is more than due for amendment and updating, for a number of reasons. However, let us discuss first what everyone in this House would agree on. Canada's effort in formulating and administering refugee policy is an essential reflection of Canada's humanitarian interests. Canadians have shown that they have the capacity to reach out to those who are suffering persecution for reasons of race, religion, or politics, and to give comfort to the homeless and stateless. Not very long ago, in 1979, Canada was setting an example to the world by urging Southeast Asian countries not to turn away boat people.
The number of people on the move in the world is increasing. It is reckoned that at any time 70 million to 80 million people are on the move. According to United Nations standards some are genuine refugees, some are unhappy, desperate people moving because of threat of war, revolution or, very often, sheer poverty in their own countries, and some have the same motivation as have immigrants- the desire to create a better life and future for themselves and their children, but they lack the skills which would make them acceptable as immigrants under the normal legislation.
Clearly Canada cannot accept 70 million or 80 million people. We must have laws which balance the needs of those unhappy people who would like to come into our country with Canada's interests. We must have laws which protect Canada's sovereignty. When the 1976 Immigration Act was discussed in this House and in committee those many different interests were balanced carefully and thoughtfully by Members on all sides of the House.
The legislation which the Government has placed before us now wants to slam the door but does not address the other matters. For instance, as long ago as 1980 there was much discussion in the United Nations about the need to find better ways to settle refugees nearer their own homes, the need to find better methods of international dispute settlement, protection of human rights, and assurance of economic prosperity in other countries. These all form basic parts of any approach to refugees and I have heard no attempt in this discussion from the Minister or Members of the other sides to pull those factors in. We only hear that this is a piece of legislation to slam the doors.
We all know that there are abuses but this Bill does not adequately deal with them. Neither does it ensure that we maintain our traditional commitment to assisting refugees. This Bill makes no attempt to involve citizens. Consider, for example, the magnificent effort at the time of the Vietnam refugees when church groups and citizen groups became

February 1, 1988

involved in assisting in the settlement of people. That was something of which we can be proud. Most of those people have gone on to become very good citizens who are contributing a lot to Canada.
We need to deal with abuses, but we certainly need to remember our traditional commitment to refugees as well. Unfortunately, this Bill does not do that.
1 might also mention that part of the reason people are being encouraged by so-called immigration consultants to misuse the refugee application system is that it is so hard to qualify as an immigrant under the existing Act. On August 12, when the Minister introduced in the House his legislation to deal with refugee abuses, he added as a sweetener that he was proposing to ease the rules so that unmarried brothers and sisters could be sponsored. Nothing has happened since then.
On January 29, the Minister issued a press release, essentially saying, "Don't call us, we'll call you". He said, "We are in the process of amending the immigration regulations", but went on to say that it would take several months. Why did the Minister raise false hopes on August 12 if he had no intention of moving for the best part of a year?
The Parliamentary Secretary opposite is an able man whom 1 respect. 1 do not think this morning's performance was typical of him, but I do not know how he can justifiably criticize us on this side of the House, complaining that we have had five days of debate about amendments, when his own Minister has had eight months in which to produce a regulation change that he promised and which is still not in force.
The commitment of the Canadian people to assisting genuine refugees still exists. Canada has never lost by it. We have gained many thoughtful contributing citizens. Our commitment to deal with those who would abuse the system must be equally strong because those who abuse the system flood it and block it.
Presently, only 10 per cent of the enormous numbers of people applying for refugee status are qualified. This means that the other 90 per cent are so blocking the system that those 10 per cent who need to get a decision and get on with organizing their lives in Canada are prevented from doing so. They are held up by a cumbersome system, and that needs to be addressed. I have no quarrel with that, but this particular Bill is limited, and the provision about turning back ships is wrong.
I hope the Minister will reconsider that amendment. 1 also hope the Minister will move on some of the other areas that he will start prosecuting so-called immigration consultants in a more vigorous fashion, that he will deal with abuses using the existing provisions of the Immigration Act and the existing provisions against fraud in the Criminal Code.

Mr. Speaker, I was very pleased to hear the Hon. Member for Trinity (Miss Nicholson) say that this
Immigration Act, 1976
country should continue its commitment to true refugees and to their admission. I hope she would agree that that is precisely what this Government has done.
I submit that in the past three years and some months since the Government took office there have been more immigrants and refugees admitted to this country than in any similar three-year period for some time.
She directed our attention particularly to the admission of boat people from southeast Asia in 1979. I remind her that that was the initiative of a Conservative Government. It was an initiative that drew support from all sectors of our society. I was glad to be among those who arranged for admission and sponsorship of one of the boat people. I agree with her that many of them have become worthy citizens of this country, including the young man to whom I referred.
I was not as impressed when the Hon. Member opposed the clause of the proposed Act which authorizes the Minister to turn back ships that are suspected of carrying bogus refugees. Last August, when 174 would-be refugees landed on our shores, her Leader said that the ship should have been turned back. He rebuked the Government for not taking the kind of initiative that would have prevented the ship from landing.
It is not the first time that we have found there is some difference of opinion between the Leader of the Liberal Party and those who purport to follow him. However, I draw to the attention of the House today's gap between leadership and commitment.
I regret very much that there continues to be the reference to this clause that we have had this morning, as on other occasions. Normally the Hon. Member for Trinity is not a fearmonger and has not been so today, but I do regret that there has been no recognition given today, as on other occasions, to the fact that the Minister, having received such authority to turn back a ship, is enabled to do so only after having due regard to the safety of the vehicle and its passengers and to the convention. It is an authority that can be used only with restraint and due recognition to the safety of those concerned.

subsubtopic: PROPOSED TWINNING OF ROCKLAND, ONT., WITH SANTA MARTA, EL SALVADOR
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on January 19, 1988, the Rockland Town Council in my constituency decided to pass a resolution in favour of twinning with the City of Santa Marta, Cabanas, El Salvador. This village was virtually depopulated in 1981 as a result of an attack that affected not only Santa Marta but the entire region. I am informed by SalvAide that 80 people were killed in that massacre and that civilians fled to Honduras in order to live in refugee camps. There, some 250 children died within the first six months as a result of the camp living conditions in question.
Finally, the people of that community decided to repopulale their community of Santa Marta. Despite insurmountable odds and with the support of the international humanitarian community, 1,645 returned to their homes in Santa Marta. subtopic: CONDITIONS IN GORONGOSA REFUGEE CAMP
CONDITIONS IN GORONGOSA REFUGEE CAMP
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have just returned from two and a half weeks in the front line states of southern Africa, Zimbabwe, Zambia, Mozambique and Botswana. There I was lucky enough to go with ZIMOFA, the Zimbabwe-Mozambique Friendship Association, into the Beira Corridor. I visited a refugee camp called Gorongosa. Eight thousand people were forced into the camp by the camp's MNR South African supported bandits. At one point 10 people a day were dying of starvation, both children and old people, because the food cannot get through.
As I speak now, the Minister for External Affairs (Mr. Clark) is in Lusaka with other Commonwealth Ministers, and I urge two practical steps on those Ministers.
First, we have to get food aid through and that means by communications and transport aid, what we call non-lethal military aid. The Minister should commit the Commonwealth to that right away.
Second, we should continue our good work through SADCC. I was able to attend the opening of the first project which was a hydro electric power project constructed by Canadian engineers.
I received a warm reception as a Canadian in southern Africa, but there are great expectations for Canada to deliver more stability and peace in the front line states are one of the


February 1, 1988

biggest blows that we and the Commonwealth can strike against the evil apartheid regime of South Africa.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, cries of the unborn are not being heard in Canada at this time because of last week's Supreme Court decision. I must express my extreme disappointment with the ruling that was handed down when five of our Justices thought it more important that every woman should have equal access to an abortion rather than have an abortion committee examine the validity of such a request.
In British Columbia there are already 25 abortions for every 100 live births. This is an appalling number, and it is sad when live fetuses are killed without any consideration given to their rights.
I call on the Minister of Justice (Mr. Hnatyshyn) and the Government to work quickly and carefully with the provinces to address how to protect the thousands of unborn humans who will continue to be murdered as a direct result of the Supreme Court decision.
Many Canadians feel that the issue of abortion is not just a legal one. It encompasses the whole idea of family and obligation. It is this that must be dealt with now.

Mr. Speaker, this afternoon at 3.30 the Minister of Employment and Immigration (Mr. Bouchard) will finally have the chance to set the record straight with respect to parental leave. He will be visited by the man who has really highlighted more than any other person the discrimination in our current maternity benefits system.

speechtext:

Today I received in the mail a delivery notice from Canada Post to pick up a parcel.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on January 28, 1988, the Supreme Court of Canada rendered its decision on the Morgentaler case by striking down Section 251 of the Criminal Code as being contrary to Section 7 of the Charter of Rights.
At the federal level this decision leaves Canada without any law on abortion from conception right up until the very


February 1, 1988

moment of birth. At the provincial level there is now health care confusion with our provinces literally going in 10 different directions.
Throughout the country there is widespread ethical debate about the fundamental issue involved. Therefore, I call upon the Government to exercise its prerogative under Section 33 of the Charter through a notwithstanding provision as an interim measure.
Further, given that all seven members of the Supreme Court indicated that Parliament has the legitimate state interest in the protection of the foetus, I call upon the Government to establish in law that the word "everyone" in Section 7 of the Charter includes the foetus or the unborn child within its mother's womb.

Mr. Speaker, the Minister of Health and Welfare (Mr. Epp) has just returned from a major international conference in London sponsored by the World Health Organization and concerned with the AIDS epidemic which will affect up to one million people over the next 10 years or so. The Minister has indicated that Canada will host a conference in Montreal one year from now.
It is very interesting that the Minister is willing to speak out and host things internationally in this respect, while he has done almost nothing at home. During the Christmas recess I had occasion to consult with leading West Coast authorities, and also received information from San Francisco. It is very evident that nothing is being done to help people who are already infected. They cannot even get through on information lines, much less get any projects considered. New drugs must be tested. Nothing is being done about that.
There is a complete lack of co-ordination between different cities, and the three major cities in Canada have considerable experience now. There is no network in place to exchange information. The National Centre for AIDS is not providing full assistance. The public at large must have mass media education.

subtopic: PROVISION OF ABORTION SERVICES BY PHYSICIANS

Mr. Speaker, the implication of the judgment of the Supreme Court of Canada is quite clear. It has rendered the present provisions of the Criminal Code with respect to abortion under Section 251 unconstitutional.

provinces in matters of health and delivery of health services. I am not sure that is the position of the Leader of the New Democratic Party in the issue. He nods that it is not.
