subtopic: IMMIGRATION ACT, 1976 MEASURE TO AMEND-CONSIDERATION OF SENATE AMENDMENTS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I listened with some interest to the debate on Bill C-84 this morning. I heard the usual over-cooked rhetoric from Members on the government side, according to whom those of us who are attempting to bring some reason, perhaps some humanity to this legislation, are filibustering. I suppose that they would make the same accusation of the Senate or of the large number of organizations which presented their points of view to the Senate.
Some 400 individuals and organizations in some manner let the Senate know their objections to this legislation. Some 37 organizations made direct representations before the Senate committee. I suppose all of these people are people who are engaged in a filibuster. They could have no other motive
except to somehow make it difficult for the Government to do good things.
Of course, you, Mr. Speaker, I am sure, as well as we, understand that there are some serious defects in this piece of legislation which is justified on the basis that there have been thousands who have abused our immigration procedures and our refugee determination processes to undermine Canadian law, to jump queues and God knows what all. What in fact has been the issue is that this legislation in its Draconian way threatens to place Canada in a position in which not only will it be in contravention of the UN Convention on Refugees but our own Charter of Rights. We have to regard these as serious questions.
The Senate listened carefully to the interventions of many Canadians, most of whom have a long established interest and concern about refugees. Many of these people have been involved in giving access to the humanitarian care that Canada provides to refugees for which we have been characterized as giving in the past. Thus we have regarded the Senate amendments as being constructively framed, not to make it difficult for the Government but to reflect the true heart of Canada.
In looking at all of the rhetoric that has issued from the other side of the House, particularly in the wake of the arrival of two boatloads of people which occasioned the introduction of this legislation, I must confess that there have been times when we have been ashamed of what we have heard from that side. Some of it has contained only slightly veiled elements of, if not racism then certainly of xenophobia which I think can do nothing but embarrass us all.
I suppose it has to be said that the events which transpired after that and the consideration of the very rapidly introduced Bill C-55 and Bill C-84, as well as the Senate's rather slower deliberations, are an object lesson in saying to a democratic institution such as our own that we should not react in a crisis situation with the first thought that comes into our heads. That has been the record of the Government in respect to its response to those episodes which has been, in effect, to come up with legislation that is essentially thoughtless and that has not given sufficiently due attention to those principles that 1 think most Canadians have long since accepted as being essential to the Canadian outlook upon the world, upon Canada itself and its citizens.
The Senate introduced a number of amendments. The first of the amendments is an interesting one. It is interesting from the point of view of the criticism of the original framing of Bill C-84 and alludes to the kind of motives and outlook which impelled this Bill into the House. That is to say the suggestion by the Senate that the wording "the assistance of clandestine entry" replace the word "smuggling" in the description of the purpose of the legislation. What the Senate noted is that "smuggling" is a word more appropriately applied to merchandise, goods or commodities. That the Government chose to describe the infraction in that term smuggling is an allusion to the kind of depersonalization which has occurred on the
February 1, 1988

government benches and in the mind of the Minister in considering the way in which the Government might properly address the problem. This is a problem that we all recognize in terms of dealing with the massive numbers of illegal immigrants who come to Canada, but which in the approach the Government has used confuses illegal immigrant with refugees.
In the fourth amendment the Senate suggests that those who have been issued security certificates not be rejected from the refugee determination system. That is to say that the Senate recognizes that because someone has been characterized as a security risk, that person does not necessarily present a serious threat to the safety of Canada or to Canadians.
Security risks may be characterized in a number of ways. For example, they may be people who, as defined in the Immigration Act, advocate the overthrow by violent means of some government or another. This is interesting because the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Clark) not too very long ago suggested that the Government might be willing to accept some Contra refugees into Canada in the wake of the culmination of the peace proposal that is now going on with respect to Nicaragua. Surely that simple fact demonstrates what should have been done by the Minister; that there are circumstances in which those who might be characterized as security risks, particularly on the evidence of another Government, may indeed be people who should have some access to refugee status and the ability to seek santuary somewhere.
If Nelson Mandela, Winnie Mandela, Bishop Tutu, or any number of Haitian dissidents were to seek refugee status under this legislation, they would find themselves in great difficulty if the refugee determination process or the effects of this legislation were to end up with such applicants being given a security certificate, that is, classified as security risks.
The United Nations recognizes the fact that such may be the case; that those who may be classified as security risks may well require a safe haven somewhere, and require that such people have access to the refugee determination process before they are deported, and that an opportunity be provided for them to seek safe haven in a safe country.
In response to the presentations and representations of a number of organizations, almost unanimous, the Senate made a suggestion for amendment to Bill C-84 which would have provided that those who have security certificates be granted access to the refugee determination system. Therefore, we find that in rejecting this amendment, the Government has again made a decision which flies in the face of consensus among those whom this Party, and I know the Official Opposition, respect as people who are presenting a case that has reason, merit, and which on the basis of the Senate amendment should have been considered a reasonable inclusion in this legislation. Indeed, we place ourselves in a rather unique category. We would join only Belgium in this provision which excludes those
Immigration Act, 1976
classified as security risks from the refugee determination system.
If we look at Senate amendment 5, which the government also rejects, which has to do with turning ships around, we find another area where the Senate has presented an amendment that this Party sees unobjectionable, indeed, which it supports, an amendment that is again supported by any number of organizations which consider that the refugee process should be a fair one.
If one looks in the legislation as it is presently written, one finds the proposed Section:
91.1(1) Where the Minister believes on reasonable grounds that a vehicle within
(a) the internal waters of Canada, (b) the territorial sea of Canada, or (c) twelve nautical miles of the outer limit of the territorial sea of Canada is bringing any person into Canada in contravention of this Act or the regulations, the Minister may, after having due regard to the safety of the vehicle and its passengers and to the convention, direct the vehicle to leave or not to enter the internal waters of Canada or the territorial sea of Canada, as the case may be, and any such direction may be enforced by such force as is reasonable in the circumstances.
The Senate rejects that proposed section. We favour the Senate position in this respect. What we are doing is creating a situation in which the Minister in some fashion determines that there are no refugees on those ships. I do not know how the Minister intends to do that. One fundamental principle of the refugee determination process is that there should be due process, that a refugee claimant should have an opportunity to have his or her claim heard.
The legislation as presently written would have the ship turned around, to what fate no one knows. Is it to be turned around in the direction of a safe country? How are we supposed to know whether it is a safe country? Indeed, is there any expectation that the ship that is turned around will go to any country? Of course, there is a very great fear that a ship's captain faced with the prospect of having to sail to God knows where with a boatload of people may indeed decided to dump them at sea. 1 do not know if the Government or any Canadian wants to be in the position of being responsible, as this legislation would have us responsible in the circumstances, for having boatloads of people dumped at sea. This is something to which Canadians have previously objected.
In fact, we recall the situation in 1939 when the St. Louis tried to approach Canadian waters to land some Jewish refugees. Other nations had also rejected them, and their fate was that they had no place to go and death was their refuge. There have been other examples in which Canada has more recently condemned the Philippines and Malaysia for having turned boats around. Now we have before us legislation which would have Canada do the same thing.
In respect to the refugee determination process, it is expected that such applicants or potential refugees will have access to a reasonable process. It is required by international convention, and it is required by Section 7 of the Charter. I know that the Minister states that as long as they do not land

February 1, 1988
Immigration Act, 1976
in a port they are not in Canada. Nevertheless, on the other hand they will be subject to Canadian law that will determine whether those boats will be turned around on the opinion of the Minister. The Government cannot have it both ways. It cannot argue that it is not subject to Section 7 of the Charter because they are not in Canada, and at the same time apply legislation to them which could lead to a fateful end of those who have sought Canada as a place of refuge.
If it is our intention to deter such effort to bring illegal immigrants, even if not refugees to Canada, surely the appropriate thing is to escort such ships into port. If the captain is guilty of breaking Canadian law, then that captain can be put in jail, fined, and have his boat forfeited. At the same time, we would have an opportunity for any legitimate refugees to have their cases heard.
It would seem to me, and to any sound thinking Canadian, that the amendment suggested by the Senate is the most appropriate. It is clear. Without too much difficulty we can apply this amendment in the practical case and bring about the appropriate solution sought by the Government. The amendment as suggested by the Senate is as follows:
91.1 Where the Minister believes on reasonable grounds that a vehicle within
(a) the internal waters of Canada, or (b) the territorial sea of Canada is bringing any person into Canada in contravention of this Act or the regulations, the Minister may direct that the vehicle be escorted to the nearest port of disembarkation and any such direction may be enforced by such force as is reasonably necessary.
What more could be desired? What could be more fitting? Bring the ship into port; try the captain and if he is found guilty, jail him. If there are illegal immigrants, deal with them in the appropriate fashion. On the other hand, if there are refugees then let them have access to the refugee determination system which is appropriate under not only the Canadian Charter of Rights but the international convention.
Finally, we have to deal with the question of aiding and abetting.
I am sure you have heard repeatedly, Mr. Speaker, that the legislation as presently written would cause any number of humanitarian people devoted to the cause of refugees to be jailed. Among the reasons they might be jailed is that refugees do not have the appropriate papers. I do not have to remind you, Mr. Speaker, that the vast majority of those who have come to this country did not come by boat in the first place. They came by airplane and had documentation of some kind or other.
It is rare for humanitarian groups devoted to the aiding of refugees to bring in such refugees in a clandestine fashion, which is something that was recognized by the Senate and ought to be recognized by the Government. I do not understand why it is not possible for anyone who thinks logically to accept the amendment as proposed by the Senate.
The following people would be guilty of a crime: every person who knowingly organizes, induces, aids or abets, or knowingly attempts to organize, induce, aid or abet a person to make a manifestly unfounded or fraudulent refugee claim, or knowingly brings or attempts to bring or otherwise knowingly organizes, induces, aids or abets, or knowingly attempts to organize, induce, aid or abet any person to come into Canada in a clandestine fashion or manner. That is what should be sought, and what would be satisfactory. That would preclude the imprisonment and prosecution of people who are trying by their sincere efforts to help those threatened in their homeland with death or torture or persecution. That amendment should have been accepted by the Government. Why it was not I do not know. It may have been pigheadedness, it may have been stubborness, it may have been stupidity, or it may have been inhumanity. However, it certainly does not reflect the views of Canadians.
Mir. Blenkarn: Mr. Speaker, does the Hon. Member feel that someone who assisted a refugee or someone to come into Canada and organized the fraud and misrepresentation to make that entry into Canada possible should in his view be subject to prosecution for aiding and abetting a breach of our Immigration Act?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the President of the Privy Council
subtopic: IMMIGRATION ACT, 1976 MEASURE TO AMEND-CONSIDERATION OF SENATE AMENDMENTS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I guess we have two kinds of filibuster in this Chamber-an intelligent filibuster based on information which Hon. Members should hear and a rhetorical filibuster based on attempt to incite, and I think we are dealing with the latter.
This is the fifth day of debate on Senate amendments. We are approaching an historic milestone in the life of Parliament. Meanwhile many other problems exist in the country. We have debated the Bill since August. However, perhaps just to emphasize the fact that the Hon. Member opposite is dealing with rhetoric rather than with intelligent comment, the situation he abhors, of being able to charge church leaders and others for organizing people, is the situation that exists in Canada right now. Until the day we change this legislation those people can be charged, can be convicted, and can suffer the penalties of that conviction. That is the legal situation today which the Government is trying to correct.
Let us come to the second part of the issue. Do we correct it? We have to look at Bill C-84 and Bill C-55 as a package.
February 1, 1988

For the first time in Canadian history Bill C-55 says clearly that anybody who breaks Canadian immigration law in any way, shape, or fashion, fraudulently or otherwise, and makes the claim to be a refugee will not be chargeable until that claim is determined. If they are found to be a refugee, they will never be charged and never be convicted. Today refugee claimants do not have that kind of protection. Without this Bill they will not have it tomorrow either. With this package of changes they will have it.
If we listen to criminal law experts on the particular clause in Bill C-84 which seems to bother the Hon. Member, we must ask ourselves whether any provincial Attorney-General will ever be able to get a conviction of somebody who organizes an activity which in itself is not illegal. Bill C-55 indicates clearly that engaging in those kinds of activities, if one is a refugee, is not to be illegal any longer. However, those who organize manifestly unfounded claimants-the 3,000 people who came from Portugal and the 1,800 who came from Brazil where there was no basis for the claim-will be chargeable under the new legislation, and they should be chargeable under the new legislation. This is why the Act is being amended.
If they want to complain, let them complain about the present legal situation. Let us get off this filibuster and let us vote. They have a right to an opinion different from that of government Members. We happen to believe that our view is the best view for refugee claimants and the best view for the country. They happen to have a different one. Let us go to a vote and move along. Let us get to some other important pieces of legislation such as that copyright. In the meantime, having come back for an emergency session in August, surely we have passed the point of rhetoric. We should be dealing with the matter in a substantive, factual, and informed way.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the repeated characterization of the debate by the Opposition as a filibuster is nothing short of despicably anti-democratic, and the people of Canada should understand it. That representative of the Government says that what I have said is rhetoric. What I say is an expression of the passion with which I reject the Government's position on this legislation.
The Hon. Member says that what a refugee may do in order to gain admission into this country after the determination of refugee status will not be construed as illegal. Once again he says that 1 am using rhetoric, but he refers to the Portugese and so on who came into the country with documents. Yet it is his legislation which would jail those who knowingly organize, induce, aid or abet, or attempt to organize, induce, aid or abet the entry into Canada of a person who is not in possession of a valid and subsisting visa. What refugee is going to come into this country with a ready-made passport and visa unless he or she is going to do it at the risk of his or her life? This is not rhetoric. This is truth. The Senate recognized the truth, as did 400 organizations which made their case to the Senate. This is not a filibuster. It is an attempt to get the Government to
Immigration Act, 1976
listen to the people who have a more sympathetic chord in their heart in respect of refugees in the world.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, 1 too want to comment on the interjections of the Parliamentary Secretary who seems to feel that by poking a stick into a cage with a grizzly bear that somehow you will get co-operation from the grizzly bear or that somehow the bear will start treating you nicer.
It is an odd way to get co-operation on the floor of the House of Commons, to be hurling insults and making accusations and then asking, "Will you co-operate?" We are the grizzly bears and they are the ones who are poking sticks. Quite frankly it is an odd approach.
Repeatedly the Parliamentary Secretary rises and says that this is a good and thoughtful piece of legislation. He says that this is a useful initiative. Of course, there are useful components of this legislation. Every single clause is not a horror show.
The point in a debate in the House of Commons on a motion is for those of us who are in Her Majesty's opposition Parties to try to identify whatever flaws may exist in legislation. As my Hon. friend for Windsor-Walkerville (Mr. McCurdy) so eloquently stated, dozens and dozens of groups with expertise and experience in this matter, people who have dedicated their lives and raison d'etre to this issue, have said repeatedly that there are serious flaws in this legislation. Various members of the Liberal and New Democratic Parties have pointed them out.
As you know, Mr. Speaker, we are simply doing our job. We are trying to convince the Parliamentary Secretary that he should not have the attitude that because his Party has a large majority of Members, it can ignore democratic traditions and the parliamentary system and just use jackboot techniques to jam any legislation through. Our parliamentary system does not withstand that kind of arrogance. I urge the Parliamentary Secretary to be thoughtful when making comments. As we attempt to improve this legislation, and hopefully not for much longer, we should be given that recognition and not be accused of filibustering legislation when that is not taking place at all.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I would like to reiterate what the Hon. Member for Kamloops-Shuswap (Mr. Riis) said. The Government, of course-

speakerposition: Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs

speechtext: That still doesn't make it true.

subtopic: IMMIGRATION ACT, 1976 MEASURE TO AMEND-CONSIDERATION OF SENATE AMENDMENTS
speechtext:
It makes it a lot truer than it was before.
The allegations made by government Members that opposition Members are filibustering this Bill are completely ridiculous. If there is any reason for the delay in this Bill, it is because the Government introduced a Bill which was completely inadequate and unsatisfactory for the purposes

February 1, 1988
Immigration Act, 1976
supposedly intended by the Government when it brought it forward.
Hon. Members will recall that this legislation was brought forward in a great hurry after a boatload of people were brought ashore in Nova Scotia this past summer. It was perceived at that time that a Bill of this kind would be popular with the people of Canada. The bringing forth of this Bill in such haste was an unfortunate response to the situation.
As has been said this afternoon, not all of this Bill is ridiculous or unnecessary. There are some very good parts to this Bill, but there are parts that need to be corrected. As long as these gaping inequities exist, it is the role of Parliament to examine them.
Such a strong supporter of the Senate as the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs (Mr. Andre) would, I am sure, realize and admit that the Senate has provided a very good service, though none of its major recommendations have been accepted by the Government. Some of the minor ones have been accepted and I think that these minor recommendations do help to strengthen the Bill and give it a great deal more credibility. I think it is unfortunate that there are some amendments that the Government has refused to acknowledge.
It has been stated already that those who knowingly aid refugees or would-be refugees to come to Canada are open to prosecution under this legislation. The way that clause is worded is unfortunate. There are people who want to bring refugees into this country who are taking a chance. They will now have to say to themselves: "We will bring these people to Canada to protect them from the danger they are facing in their own countries and we will risk prosecution in order to do so. There is a bad law and we must ask ourselves if we will aid these people and be subject to the bad law or, on the other hand, if we will not aid these people and play it safe".
These people who have the benefit of their fellow men at heart will take the risk of being prosecuted because they are helping refugees. These people who want to help their fellow men are not criminals. They are not people who will falsify documents or lie, but they will help people in need.
To say that refugees must have passports or visas when they arrive in Canada is completely ludicrous. Refugees who are in difficulty and fear for their lives in their own countries have to leave very quickly and do not have a chance to obtain proper documentation before leaving.
It is important to ask what kind of image we want to portray as a country. Of course, we do not want to portray Canada as being a place where anyone who wants to leave his own country for whatever reason can come. That is not the point, but it is important that Canada maintain its image of being a country that helps those people who are in genuine difficulty in their own land and who were trying to make their own country a better place and therefore fear for their own safety.
What is the Government doing about all this? Of course, the Government is taking a very stand-pat position on this Bill. It
is saying that even though it was brought in in haste and without proper thought, the Government will not make any changes to it because it does not want to tip its hand any more than it already has by acknowledging that it brought this Bill forward without proper thought. Of course, the Government is hoping that Canadians do not see the inadequacies, inconsistencies and inequities in this legislation.
One particular clause of this Bill typifies the problems that exist with this legislation. It is the clause which gives the Government the right to turn back vessels that are possibly bringing people into Canada illegally. The Bill provides that this must be done with the approval of the Minister and talks about possibilities that are very slim and probably will not happen. A very real possibility exists that this will happen, but this cannot be tolerated in our society.
We are not only talking about refugees or people who come into Canada illegally, we are talking about the rights of individuals. I do not think it is right for the Government of Canada to take a position of us and them. The Government is saying that those who are Canadian citizens are one type and those who are not Canadians are another type and are not of the same status and do not have rights. 1 believe that that is wrong.
If we go along with that, we are saying that we agree with the Government's position. If we agree with the Government's position, we will start the downward slide in our high standards of human rights. No sooner will we have agreed with the Government's position on reducing the rights of these people who would come into Canada legally or illegally than we would be saying that human rights abuses in other countries can go on. We will start turning a blind eye to these abuses. Then we will start saying that no one is a refugee because if a person is a citizen of another country, that person has a responsibility to that other country. Gradually, we will become more callous in our thinking toward our fellow man. To me, that is the real threat in this piece of legislation. Then we come back inside our own borders and start eating away at the rights of Canadians. Soon the very people who have agreed to the whittling away of rights of people from other countries begin to see their own rights whittled away. That is the inevitable consequence of treating some more fairly than others.
Turning a vessel away in this situation is not fair treatment of our fellow man. Second, it is not the answer the Government says it is. The people who have organized this sailing for profit will be allowed to get away, only to turn around and do it again with another boatload of people. Third, to set those people adrift outside Canadian waters in goodness knows what kind of conditions and in what kind of vessel would be a travesty.
I ask you, what happens to those people then? Do we allow them to bob around the ocean in an unsafe vessel? Do we allow
February 1, 1988

them to just stay there, men, women and children? Undoubtedly, over the course of time, they will reach the shore anyway, the fortunate ones. The unfortunate ones will perish at sea. Is that what the Government wants?
That is completely unsatisfactory. It is no answer at all. It does not deal with those who break the law and profit from the misery of these people. The better solution would be to bring the vessel into port and charge the person in control. Make sure that person is penalized to the full extent of the law. More important, we would make sure those people, whether they are true refugees or not, at least have a safe haven while their case is being decided.
What is wrong with giving them the benefit of the doubt? What is wrong with bringing them ashore and applying Canadian law? The law is here, why push them away? Why devise laws for these people and then drive them from Canadian waters and not apply the law? It makes no sense whatsoever.
We have to give some real thought to this. We have to reflect on it once again. To say that this Bill is being filibustered is not adequate. What kind of alternative do we get? We have heard two or three cases during the life of this Government involving people who had the money to get into Canada even though they did not have the proper qualifications. They did not have the proper background or had committed acts in their country which, under ordinary circumstances, would not make them eligible for Canadian visas or landed immigrant status. There seems to be a double standard.
We have to look at the true situation. The true situation is that all the people who land in Canada deserve to have Canadian law applied to them. You cannot say that because they come here by boat their right to Canadian law is any less important than that of someone who lands by plane or who comes across a bridge from the U.S. The law applies to people who come to Canada regardless of the method. It is here to help them. It is here to strengthen the fabric of this country.
There is no need to try and to belittle the Opposition who feels there are inconsistencies in this Bill and provisions which whittle away at the fabric of this country. We feel there is something to be said for Canada's role in the international forum and this is what we want to bring forward. That is very important, along with the rights of humanity.
I congratulate the Senate for its reflection on this Bill and the amendments agreed to by the Senate committee. They were agreed to not just by Liberal members of that committee but by all members. I think that is very important. It says a great deal about the workings of the committee. They dealt with it in an unbiased and unpartisan manner. To allege political partisanship does not do justice to the role of Parliament in dealing with this very important piece of legislation.

Mr. Speaker, I am a little surprised that someone who is usually so thoughtful, and who comes from a province with ocean borders, would so easily buy the prepared notes which have probably been done by someone who is landlocked using testimony that comes out of Toronto. Reading time after time in this House from that same set of notes is an attempt to give them credibility and contribute to what 1 have characterized as a rhetorical filibuster. It is not an informed filibuster but a rhetorical filibuster.
The Hon. Member spent a lot of time talking about the boats. I would like to spend a minute or two talking about the boats.
Maritime law, as he should know, currently allows ships to be taken into custody within your territorial limits and escorted to port. Nothing has changed. That power exists today, it will exist tomorrow, and nothing we are debating in this Chamber changes that. What did that law standing alone produce? It produced peddlers in human flesh who put people on unsafe boats in the North Atlantic. It produced another group of peddlers of flesh who brought an unsafe vessel, not a passenger vessel but an unsafe vessel crammed with people, with inadequate sanitation, health care and food, and so on, not to a port but to a rocky shore. Those who say, "Leave them all alone" are inviting a continuation of profit for peddlers in human flesh who put desperate people's lives at risk. This is really what they are arguing for time after time. They are saying that the law should not be changed because it provides the opportunity to peddle in flesh and put people's lives and health at risk.
Through changing the law we seek an additional power rather than a replacement power. We want the Minister to have the power, when satisfied as to health, safety, and refugee convention, to turn a boat back. If the penalty for ships' owners when caught is confiscation and imprisonment, are they more likely to put people in lifeboats outside our limit? Operating on the assumption that humanity does exist in those ships' captains, those peddlars, if you give the Minister the power simply to turn the boat around rather than putting the captain in prison and confiscating the boat, are they more or less likely to put people in lifeboats on the North Atlantic?
Surely the option produces the best results for the people about whom the Opposition continually says it cares. The present law put the Tamils in the lifeboats. The present law put the people in the boat on the rocky shore. It is time to be reflective. It is time to end this nonsensical filibuster.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is obvious the debate has not gone on long enough because the Hon. Parliamentary Secretary to the Deputy Prime Minister (Mr. Hawkes) has said that even though he has heard it many times it still has not penetrated. I hope that if we say it a few more times it will penetrate.

February 1, 1988
Immigration Act, 1976
The Bill does go further than the existing law. To say that the Bill is only intended to give another avenue to the Minister is just not correct. This legislation would blatantly put the welfare of the people who would be the cargo in these vessels out of the window without any regard for them whatsoever. To turn a vessel around it would have to be in Canadian waters.
The fact is that it is much better to seize the vessel in order that the cargo will at least be in your protection. You will have boarding rights which will enable you to learn the condition of the people. You will at least have a chance to help them. If the people are in desperately bad health and on the verge of succumbing to the rigours of the voyage, you can do something for them. You could airlift them and give them immediate treatment. If you turn them around, they are sentenced to certain death.
In the interests of human beings there is no choice. You must do what you can. You do not put people in prison and starve them to death simply because they are illegal. You do not subject them to inhumane treatment just because they are criminals. Even if these people are criminals and are coming into Canada illegally they are entitled to humane treatment. That is what we ask for-humane treatment.

Mr. Speaker, I appreciated very much the response which the Member made to the last question and I agree with him completely. I would like to ask him a question which has been bothering me for some time.
The Member will recall the days after the Vietnamese War when people from Southeast Asia were in boats at sea and their lives were in danger. Many of them had paid people for their passage and were what the Member referred to as the human cargo on these little boats.
The ASEAN countries; Thailand, Indonesia, and Malaysia, took them in and were the countries of first refuge. If we apply what Canada is trying to do with this legislation to the situation there, those ASEAN countries would have applied all those prohibitions and those people would have been left at sea.
Is that a fair analogy? Would the Member like to comment on that? It is wonderful that those countries, which are so poor
themselves, took in those refugee claimants. They still have many of them in camps and Canada refuses to take them.

subtopic: IMMIGRATION ACT, 1976 MEASURE TO AMEND-CONSIDERATION OF SENATE AMENDMENTS

Mr. Speaker, I would be very pleased to reply to that. That is a lesson we learned which the Government has obviously not remembered. This country took in thousands of Vietnamese boat people, as they were called at that time, even though they were not floating in Canadian waters. Canada's record has been tremendous in that regard because of our concern for the lives and welfare of these people. They were in camps in Southeast Asian countries in the best conditions which those countries could provide.
The Government of Canada moved quickly and instituted a fifty-fifty policy with private groups. Areas of this country which were not as economically strong as others participated. Groups in Newfoundland, Cape Breton, and from coast to coast sponsored these people to come to Canada. speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this Bill has been reported from the other place and the amendments suggested there were unanimously passed by the members of that place. They felt so strongly about it that they endorsed the recommendations to humanize this Bill. That is the key to this extra opportunity which the Government has to deal with this issue. The Senate has given the Government an opportunity to deal with the Bill once more.
Good legislation goes through without too much debate. Bad legislation keeps turning up. The Senate has given the Government an opportunity to improve this Bill in a humanitarian way. This legislation is bad in a number of ways. It turns away boats as they enter Canadian waters. That has been recognized by many people on both sides of the House as a dangerous situation. This may turn away legitimate refugees in the process, without giving them the opportunity for a hearing in Canada. That runs against the traditions and practice of Canadian immigration policy for many years.
Canada is a country of immigrants. We come from a background of people who left their homes to come to Canada in search of a better life with greater opportunities. We have had a tradition of accepting refugees who wanted to take advantage of the greater opportunities that our parents had. If this Bill adopted, we may turn away legitimate refugees without the benefit of a hearing.
Second, those who profit from the plight of refugees by transporting them by boat would be forced to drop potential refugees outside the 200-mile boundary, leaving it up to them to make it to shore. Would it not be more useful to seize the ship, and put out of commission these rip-off artists and
February 1, 1988

unscrupulous agencies who profit from refugees? Would it not be more useful to confiscate their vessels so they can no longer carry on such practices?
The Senate has done the Government a service by giving it another opportunity to correct the legislation. It had the opportunity to make this a more humanitarian Bill when it was first introduced to the House. Humanitarianism is the key element forgotten in this Bill. There is ample opportunity in Canada for everyone to have the kind of full and productive life that refugees want. Canada has great wealth, with many opportunities for an almost limitless number of people. It is wrong to prevent such an opportunity by ignoring the basics of humanitarian treatment.
There are two key elements of the Bill to which we object. The Government has refused to address the question of authority to detain identified refugee claimants for long period without review. It has also retained the right to turn back ships at sea, thereby preventing humanitarian treatment of people attempting to get into Canada.
The amendments with which we are dealing today suggest that as much opportunity as possible be given to these people to have access to a legal process which allows them the right to a hearing in Canada. Such a provision would allow us to live up to the reputation we have built over many years. It will fulfil the traditions on which this country was built.
Another area of concern is the treatment of people who help refugees get into this country. The Government has another opportunity to deal with this issue in a much more meaningful way. 1 think it is important that the Government use this opportunity to take the proper steps as suggested by our Party and others and reinforced by the Senate. It should change the Bill so that it is more acceptable to the people of Canada.

Mr. Speaker, I want to congratulate the Hon. Member for Prince Albert (Mr. Hovdebo) for the concern that he has shown over the years for the plight of the downtrodden and the oppressed.
I would like to follow up on the questions that were asked by the Parliamentary Secretary as well as the Hon. Member for York Centre (Mr. Kaplan) with respect to turning ships around. The Member from Prince Albert made reference to this issue. 1 note in the report from the other place there is background reference to this issue. Of course, the Senate, in making recommendations for changes in this area, looked at a couple of important arguments. The Senators looked at the questions of our international obligations and how they impact of the Charter of Rights.
In that light, the Senate is saying that it is difficult to imagine how Canada could, in fact, be seen to be adhering to its international obligations in turning a ship away, although Bill C-84 does state that the convention relating to the status of refugees is to be taken into account.
In the few minutes remaining, I would like to ask the Member to comment on the importance that the Member attaches to Canada adhering to its international obligations and also to the importance of adhering to our obligations under Section 7 of the Charter of Rights and Freedoms. By turning a ship around without allowing the basic due process to refugee claimants on board, the Senate suggests that it is quite possible that we would be in breach of the provisions of Section 7 of the Charter of Rights.
The argument made by departmental officials is that the rights under the Charter apply to people at a port of entry and not at sea. As the Hon. Member for Prince Albert knows, and he has spoken on this on a number of occasions, this matter is not at all resolved. I believe the Hon. Member has made reference in the past to the Supreme Court of Canada's decision in the case of Singh v. the Minister of Employment and Immigration in which the Supreme Court of Canada held that the protection of the Charter extends to every human being who is physically present in Canada and by virtue of such presence amenable to Canadian law. Thus, of course, refugee claimants can invoke the Charter.
The issue as to whether a claimant who has not yet landed in Canada but is in Canadian waters was not specifically before the court in the Singh case. The Hon. Member will be aware that Canada has played a positive and constructive role in the past in this area, and this particular legislation is a significant step backwards.
The Member knows, for example, that Canada set a positive example for the rest of the world in 1979 and 1980 when we urged the countries of Southeast Asia not to turn away the boatloads of refugees fleeing from those countries. I might say as well that the Hon. Member for Hamilton Mountain (Ms. Dewar) played a truly outstanding role of leadership in the community here in Ottawa in helping to resettle those particular individuals.
Would the Hon. Member for Prince Albert in the short time remaining care to comment on the importance of Canada adhering not only to our international obligations but as well to our obligations under the provisions of the Charter of Rights and Freedoms?

subtopic: IMMIGRATION ACT, 1976 MEASURE TO AMEND-CONSIDERATION OF SENATE AMENDMENTS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, most Canadians have been able in the past to point with pride to the fact that we do recognize the rights of human beings all over the world. We recognize our international obligations in accepting legitimate refugees from all parts of the world to the extent where we accepted an award for our understanding in accepting refugees when they came to our shores. If we abrogate those traditions, the Charter and our international obligations, we are stepping backwards. We are going back to the time when many parts of the world felt that they had the right to say no to refugees who had a legitimate reason for entering a country.
The tradition of refugee status is a longtime tradition which international law has accepted for many, many years. It behooves us to take care that we are not one of the nations which breaks that international obligation and the opportunity to show ourselves as believing in the Charter of Rights which we have accepted in our Constitution.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, we are dealing here with the Senate amendments to Bill C-84, a Bill dealing in the area of immigration with the restriction and entry into Canada and accelerated removal of refugees claimants. The Hon. Member for Calgary West (Mr. Hawkes) has risen throughout the debate in the last few hours to try to characterize what we are doing here in the House as a filibuster, to say that all the points have been made and that it is now time to put the question. Far from it. In this debate I submit that every Member has a duty to speak. Each of us has to stand up to tell the country why we feel that the oppressive majority which the Conservatives represent in the House should not be allowed to prevail on this Bill.
Is it not interesting that in the Senate not only do the Liberal Senators find this Bill oppressive and unacceptable but the Conservative Senators have joined them to urge on the important government amendments to Bill C-84 which is now before the House? I think that we would be derelict in our duty as Members if we did not all stand up and loudly and clearly repeat the message that has come virtually unanimously from the Senate that this Bill with the oppressive features which it contains, which I will refer to in a moment, has no place in the law books of Canada. No matter how right-wing the Government is or how motivated it is by the back-bench club which has stood up against some of the most progressive institutions in our country, there is a Charter of Rights and Freedoms and a voice in the country that will not let this Bill pass.
I want to say something about the context of the legislation, and to talk about our history for a moment. I would also like to talk about some of the other legislation on the books that, in my view, covers adequately in most respects the situation of illegal immigrants and those whom for proper reasons, the Government may wish to remove from Canada. For the sake of history I would like to point out that probably more than any other country in the world Canada is a country of refugees. It is more a country of refugees than the United States, Vietnam, China or the frontier countries of first reception where refugees flee from unsatisfactory situations within their own borders.
Recently, I saw some statistics with respect to this point. They show that in 1985 one out of every 329 Canadians is in Canada as a refugee. That does not refer to their parents or to their grandparents but to each one of 329 individuals. If we look at the 1920s and the 1930s when Ukrainians came to Canada in such large numbers to seek refuge, and to the postSecond World War years when so many others came from Europe, and to the Vietnamese refugees, it is clear that the voice of the refugee and the descendant of the refugee is a strong part of our national heritage.
When I hear the Hon. Member for Calgary West challenge us to find another country in which refugees are treated better,
1 do not think that is good enough. I know that it can be done.
Immigration Act, 1976
However, I think that the challenge is to ensure that our best humanitarian tradition is preserved in our law.
At the same time as I say that, there is another feeling in the country which is very important and which deserves respect, too. That is to say that no one in Canada likes to see us made suckers of, or likes to see the country used by people who are not refugees and who have no legitimate claim to come or to remain here but who come and look through our laws and at the humanitarian impulses of Canadians to try to find some basis to stay here. Part of our history, too, is openness and fairness toward refugees. At the same time this is not wanting to be abused or to be taken advantage of.
1 would like to turn for a moment to some of the other legislation which is available under our present laws for dealing with those who claim to be refugees. It is an interesting day for me to do so because earlier today in Question Period I asked the Minister of Employment and Immigration (Mr. Bouchard) a question about the claim to remain in Canada of Mahmoud Issa Mohammad who has been taken by the Government to court in a deportation process. An adjournment was granted until February 16 in this case. Mr. Mahmoud Issa Mohammad is by his own admission the individual who, with accomplices back in 1968 fired on an El A1 aircraft. In front of me I have a clipping from The Globe and Mail of December 27, 1968, which reports on this incident. He is the individual who fired in a terrorist attack on an El A1 airliner in Greece. According to the clipping there were 47 passengers on board and a crew.
Mr. Mahmoud Issa Mohammad was arrested, charged and convicted for that incident. Events revealed show that he was released subsequently on an exchange made to release hostages who were being held in another country. It seems pretty clear that he did not serve the sentence that was imposed upon him. When he came to Canada he admits that he concealed his record and lied about his background in order to be allowed to enter Canada as a landed immigrant.
The Minister of State for Immigration (Mr. Weiner) rose to say that our country would not become a haven for terrorists when he was asked about this matter a few days ago. He suggested that very strong measures would be taken because there are strong measures under the laws of Canada to do everything the Government can do to have Mr. Mohammad removed.
One can imagine how Canadians feel when they see a story such as that unfolding and how they would want to be certain that the laws were effective and that something could be done to remove an individual such as Mr. Mohammad who, by misrepresentation, obtained landed immigrant status. When they learn from the Minister that it will take months and years-and a departmental official, unnamed, said in the media that it could take five years to remove him-it is no wonder that some Canadians think that we need a law such as Bill C-84 on the books to give us the ammunition needed for

February 1, 1988
Immigration Act, 1976
dealing with people who come in and try to take advantage of our lax immigration laws.
That brings me to the question that I asked in the House today. All of this is very relevant because it goes to show that a tough Bill such as Bill C-84 is not really needed. In my question I referred to another part of a law of Canada, that is, to Sections 39 and 40 of the Immigration Act, as amended in 1984. I will not read the statute although 1 will refer interested Members to Section 39 of the Act, wherein there is a summary procedure for dealing with an individual found in the country other than a Canadian citizen who is in violation of the important parts of Section 19 of the Immigration Act.
When the Minister of Immigration and the Solicitor General (Mr. Kelleher) are of the opinion that such an individual has been found in Canada, and I suggest that Mr. Mohammad would certainly fit within that definition, a certificate can be issued. A summary procedure would have been available under the present legislation, which, in due course, depending on the evidence, could have led to the deportation of an individual like the one I have been describing.
# (1630)
This procedure does not deny natural justice to the individual. There is provision for a hearing. An individual can be represented by counsel. He has the right of appeal if he is dissatisfied with the result of this procedure. Yet the Government has chosen not to use this procedure, but to rely on a procedure involving the Immigration Appeal Board, involving the possibility of appeal to the Federal Court for review, and as one of the Minister's own officials stated, to a procedure that could permit an individual to remain in our country for five years.
I assure Hon. Members that I am not going to attribute improper motives to the Government. But I wish to ask the simple question, why not use a summary procedure rather than a long drawn out procedure? Does that have anything to do with Bill C-84, which the Government is trying to convince the House that it needs now? The Minister of Immigration answered me by stating that they had looked at the procedures available and decided to take the slower, more studied and deliberate procedure which they chose, rather than the one that is provided in Sections 39 and 40 of the Act.
I want to put it to the Government to use the procedures that we have now rather than coming forward with the very controversial measures contained in Bill C-84, measures which are dubious at best and which are inconsistent with our tradition as a country that is receptive to refugees, but at the same time respectful of the rule of law in not wanting to provide asylum, as some other countries do, to just anyone. We want to be certain that those to whom we provide asylum are basically law-abiding and do not violate the clauses contained in Section 19 of the Immigration Act.
My colleagues have put forward some of the difficulties that we have with this legislation. They are highlighted by the treatment given to the legislation in the Senate. I find it totally unacceptable that the Government seeks to arrogate to itself the authority to turn back a vessel. Turning back a vessel on the high seas takes a very great deal for granted. It takes for granted the fact that the people on the boat are not legitimate refugees. That should not be taken for granted. They should be entitled to a hearing. A summary procedure can certainly be applied to it. But there may be individuals on that vessel who deserve to be considered as refugees and who are refugees. They can come to Canada and make a useful contribution. If returned to their country of origin, or even to the place where they embarked on the vessel, which could be a different place from their country of origin, they may find their lives in danger.
I tell the Government, the Liberal members of the Senate and the Conservative members of the Senate tell the Government, that as Canadians we do not want to take that risk. We do not want to place individuals, who come under our responsibility as they approach Canadian shores, in that type of jeopardy. We object to the procedure which permits the boat to be turned back. We insist that there are summary procedures that are available for dealing with individuals, for giving them a right to be heard by an independent tribunal and a very summary right of appeal once they land in Canada.
A person might argue that that means that people will take shots on Canada, and that those who are not entitled to come into Canada as refugees will come anyway knowing that the boat has to land. I challenge that. If one looks at the situations in the past with the boats that have landed, the Prime Minister indicated that everyone on board was going to be allowed to stay. If that is the policy, then people will want to come. Boats will want to risk coming to Canada in the hope that they will receive that type of treatment by the Government of the day. But if they know that if they are not qualified there is a very summary procedure which will result in their being returned to the place from which they came within a short compass of days or weeks, not months or years, then they will not come in the first place. They do not come free. They have to pay to come. They have to make arrangements to come. They take a certain risk when they come and put themselves in a boat not knowing as much as they might like to about the safety record of the boat and about the intentions of the captain. It is a risky business to come in a boat. If people know that unless they are a bona fide refugees they will only be able to stay in Canada for a very short period of time, then they will not take those risks. There is no good argument for turning back the boat, which the Government proposes to take for itself in this legislation.
There is another reason why turning back the boat is unacceptable. There may be terrible hardships on the passengers on the return voyage. There is no assurance that the captain would not have needed to land for water or food. Whether or not the individuals are refugees by their original
February 1, 1988

definition, by passing this Bill we can put them in a terrible situation where they could actually be in a life threatening situation as a result of being turned back.
The Senate is correct. In his opening statement my colleague, the Hon. Member for York West (Mr. Marchi), was correct. The Government is wrong to insist that it needs this type of power.
It is unacceptable to criminalize the non-profit humanitarian activities of individuals and groups, including religious groups, for example, churches, ashrams, mosques and synagogues, that, on a benevolent basis, might come forward and offer to try to assist strangers among them without necessarily knowing the character of their arrival and the character of their claims. It is quite wrong and unworthy of a Canadian Government, and it is out of keeping with our heritage to characterize and criminalize that type of humanitarian activity and intervention by those groups.
Having had a rebuke from the Senators of their own Party, as well as from the Liberal Senators and from the Opposition united on this Bill, I urge the Government to reconsider its rejection of that portion of the Bill. Let us not criminalize those humanitarian groups among us which come forward and want to help. Let us not put them in a position where they have to go and see their lawyer, or check out with the police whether it is possible to help this group that has come on shore, for example, in the situation of the Tamils a few months back.
I wish to conclude by reminding the Government about the reaction that this Bill has engendered across the country. Perhaps the Government thought that it was on to something good. Certainly, the BBC, the Back-Benchers' Club, with a strict right-wing agenda, would have been happy to see harsh measures for wrongdoers. But this Bill goes much further than imposing harsh measures to deal with wrongdoers. It is an insensitive Bill that establishes a wall which is bound to trap deserving refugees. This country resonates with refugees and with the sense of the cause of the refugee. This Bill should not pass.

That tradition was recognized by the United Nations in 1985 when Canada received the highest possible award, the Nansen Medal, in recognition of our tradition of compassion and understanding. subtopic: PRIVATE MEMBERS BUSINESS-MOTIONS   CONSTITUTION ACT, 1982 SUGGESTED AMENDMENT TO INCLUDE PROPERTY RIGHTS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, that issue of property rights has been a personal concern of mine for at least a decade.

February 1, 1988
Property Rights
In 1979, when I ran for the first time as a Conservative, a group of Quebec candidates adopted as their basic political position, almost as a prerequisite to running for the Conservative Party, that property rights become part of any Progressive Conservative elections platform. As for my Party itself, it has had that concern for decades. We are all aware of the efforts made by the Right Hon. John Diefenbaker on the matter of property rights.
Now, Mr. Speaker, what is involved is not simply a matter of lofty principles, but rather practical matters. We know very well for instance that property rights are part of the balance between community and individual rights. Let me explain. The community of course has a right, as a society, to a healthy, positive development, but the individual also has the right to basically protect the principles inherited along with citizenship.
In 1981, during the Constitutional debate, Hon. David Crombie, now a Minister but then a backbencher, although not backward because he had very progressive ideas, stated on February 18, 1981: "Secondly, the Charter of Rights does not include property, as I mentioned earlier. The right to enjoy property is essential to people understanding not only of their rights but of their freedom and security. We put a motion to include property as a right; and it was voted down". The Hon. Member then to criticized the approach taken by the New Democratic Leader when he suggested the Charter of Rights had to be enacted as put forward because of the need for change. And the Hon. Member went on to say: "The Leader of the New Democratic Party (Mr. Broadbent) said it is time for a decision, time for change. We have to act decisively in history".
As you see, Mr. Speaker, this principle was of major concern to many responsible members of our party.
I also want to quote the comments made by the Speaker of this House, the Hon. John A. Fraser, who was then Member for Vancouver South. He was asking the then Prime Minister, Mr. Pierre Elliot Trudeau, why, knowing that it would be useless to attempt negotiating to incorporate property rights in the Constitution, the Sollicitor General, acting as Justice Minister, had made such a commitment. He also asked: "Is the Prime Minister really trying to make us believe that it was put forward to broaden consensus which the Prime Minister knew perfectly well did not exist?" I should add that the major issue of the day was to broaden consensus among the Opposition Parties. The Right Hon. Pierre Elliot Trudeau had replied: "Madam Speaker, the federal Conservative party seems to attach such importance to this matter" At which point someone had interjected: "You're damned right we do". To which Mr. Trudeau had replied: "The hon. member says, "You're damned right we do". I say that if they want that amendment so badly in the constitution, and they want it so badly that it should bind all the provinces as well as the federal government, then let them come and support us and maybe I will give up the support of the NDP." He was therefore willing to trade on a basic principle.
Mr. Fraser had then replied: "Madam Speaker, I remind the Prime Minister that the Conservative proposal is to put these provisions that we have been suggesting and working on to the provinces." In other words, we wanted the support of the provinces for a very basic principle because our party believed in the rights of the provinces as it believes in the rights of the individual.
As for Mr. Hamilton, who was then Member for Qu'Appelle-Moose-Mountain, he said the following in his speech on February 23, 1981: "The third point 1 wanted to mention was the right to enjoy property, which is the first item in the Diefenbaker Bill of Rights. Why any Liberal or NDPer would deliberately, in full public glare of television, radio and newspaper, stand up and declare that they did not want this entrenched in the Constitution is beyond me. Anyone who knows the history of the new world, South America, North America, Australia and New Zealand knows why people came to these lands. They came to enjoy the ownership of land. To the working man, that means his home."
Vince Dantzer, who was representing the Okanagan North riding at the time, stated on March the 2nd, 1981: "There are other flaws in this document, flaws due to the process and haste which has characterized the passage of this resolution. Where are property rights?
During the committee hearings the hon. member for Provencher proposed the following amendment: Freedom from unreasonable interference with privacy, family, home, correspondence and enjoyment of property. These basic rights have been accepted in our tradition for hundres of years. They appear in the Magna Carta. They were present in John Diefenbaker's bill of rights. Yet, the Liberal majority at the direction of the New Democratic Party retreated from the position of acceptance to one of rejection and refused to allow the charter to guarantee the right of Canadians to own and enjoy property. "A man's home is his castle", but not in Canada under a Liberal and NDP government." It is rather ironic, Mr. Speaker, because these days, the idea of a Canada under a Liberal and NPD Government is again fashionable.
Canadians could then remember that at that time, such a government prevented them from enjoying the right of property which is a very basic right, not only as a principle, but also as an economic right.
Everybody knows that the citizen who owns his own house, who has the joy and pride of possessing assets, will respect them, respect himself and his neighbour much more.
On the other hand, we often realize, when watching TV or reading the papers and magazines, the great many social and basic problems faced by people forced to live in the tenement sections of ghettos, such as those found in the major American cities, where a great many individuals, because they do not own any property or their own house, feel dehumanized and show the most complete disrespect for themselves, their neighbours and the premises they live in.
February 1, 1988

Personally, Mr. Speaker, I feel that this old principle should be enshrined in the Constitution, but it is also something quite practical for us Canadians, because, as 1 said, it ensures the balance between the rights of the community and the rights of individual Canadian men and women.

subtopic: PRIVATE MEMBERS BUSINESS-MOTIONS   CONSTITUTION ACT, 1982 SUGGESTED AMENDMENT TO INCLUDE PROPERTY RIGHTS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, Canadians should not be concerned in any way about the fact that property rights are not enshrined in the Charter of Rights. We have lived and now live under jurisprudence which has established an unwritten basis in law for property rights. Anglo-Canadian jurisprudence has traditionally recognized as a fundamental freedom the right of an individual to own and enjoy property, and the right not to be deprived of that property. This was established without being written into the Constitution.
Therefore, Canadians should not be concerned that property rights are not enshrined in the Charter of Rights and Freedoms. Their rights of property remain sound regardless of whether or not they are in the Charter. In fact, many countries believe that countries such as Canada, which have developed their law structure from the British parliamentary system and the British law structure and have established recognized rights, are in a better position than those which have them written into a charter such as is suggested here. When you include such rights in a charter, because it is sometimes necessary to abrogate those rights in some way, you have to make exceptions to them. As those exceptions develop the rights become less free than they would be if they were not written.
The Anglo-Canadian right to property has been confirmed by a Supreme Court decision. The Supreme Court came down firmly on the side of property rights. While they are not enshrined in the Constitution they are definitely the rights of the country.
Section 26 of the Charter of Rights and Freedoms states:
The guarantee in this Charter of certain rights and freedoms shall not be
construed as denying the existence of any other rights and freedoms that exist
in Canada.
The Charter of Rights and Freedoms specifically set out that the fact that the rights of property are not included in the Charter of Rights and Freedoms does not mean that they do not exist. There is nothing in the Charter of Rights and Freedoms which says that these rights do not exist. That is the basis upon which we in Canada live with the security that the property we own is there for our enjoyment.
This therefore seems like a little bit of overkill. Perhaps it is playing a little bit on the fears which people have of government and of what they see across the border where property rights are a little more subservient to the Government. Countries around the world look upon our situation with envy because we feel secure in our property rights and can fight
Property Rights
them in the courts without any suggestion that they are not secure.
In the process of discussing property rights we should also look at the history of Canada. We are in a rather unique situation in that when we brought our Constitution back we had the opportunity to decide what would be in it and what would be in the Bill of Rights. In the process of looking at what had happened over a period of 100 years the Parliament of the day accepted a Charter of Rights which did not include the right to enjoy property because it appeared to that Parliament, as it appeared to many people across the country, not to be necessary. In fact, the two strongest advocates of not including property rights in the Constitution were the then Premier of Alberta, Lougheed, and the then Premier of Prince Edward Island, MacLean-one a Conservative, one a Liberal. The third Premier who came down against the inclusion of property rights was Premier Blakeney of Saskatchewan. In the discussions regarding property rights in the Constitution the position of not including property rights was supported by a Conservative Premier, a Liberal Premier, and a New Democratic Premier, and by the parliamentarians at that time.

I want to confirm that Canadians should not be concerned in any way about the fact that property rights are not enshrined in the Charter of Rights and Freedoms. Property rights have existed for 100 years in Canada and for several hundred years in the British tradition around the world. They have been challenged in courts and have never failed to be upheld. Consequently, I do not believe it is necessary to put property rights in the Charter of Rights and Freedoms.

One of the two reasons I did not vote for the Constitution Act in 1982 was the fact that property rights were not included. The other reason was that the Charter of Rights and Freedoms gave no protection to unborn human beings. Many of us in the House at that time were very upset by those omissions in the Charter. We can see today, as a result of the decision brought down by the Supreme Court of Canada on Thursday, January 28, that unborn human beings are more and more discriminated against by not being included in the Charter of Rights and Freedoms. The Government of the day had no intention at any time to include unborn human beings in the Charter.
However, with regard to property rights, the Government of the day did in fact originally include property rights in the Constitution but later rescinded them. We later learned that

February 1, 1988
Property Rights
the Government bowed to the wishes and pressures of the New Democratic Party to remove property rights from the final text of the Constitution. We know why the NDP took this action, Mr. Speaker. Members of the New Democratic Party were being true to their belief that all property should be owned by the state. The NDP believes that the state knows what is best and that the people of Canada should follow their lead with no questions asked. God help us if by some accident of fate the NDP ever came to national power. It would be a disaster of the greatest magnitude.
Denying the right to private property to Canadians certainly makes a mockery of the existing rights to life, liberty, and security of person as depicted in the Charter of Rights and Freedoms.
The member of the New Democratic Party said that the definition of property is very complicated. I agree with that. We have real property which relates to land and we have personal property that deals with everything from cars to negotiable instruments. Just because the definition of property is very broad and it will, of necessity, have to be interpreted by the courts, is no reason not to embark on that course to have property rights included within the Charter of Rights and Freedoms.
At the outset, I would like to emphasize that in my view property rights have played a central role in the evolution of our society. Indeed, property rights are an essential part of British parliamentary democracy. These rights can be traced back to King John, the year 1215, with the signing of the Magna Carta.
Today, the right to own, use and enjoy property is fundamental to the economic life of our country and of other western democracies. For these reasons I believe property rights should be enshrined in the Charter of Rights and Freedoms.
The role of property in the economy of our country, the right to own, to use and to enjoy property, is fundamental to the basic feature of democracy, which is individual freedom. The Progressive Conservative Party has had a long and honourable association with this idea.
It was a Conservative Government under the late Right Hon. John G. Diefenbaker who, in 1960, introduced the Canadian Bill of Rights which included protection for the enjoyment of property. In the recent process leading to the patriation of the Constitution, it was the Progressive Conservative Party again that wanted the inclusion of property rights.
Unfortunately, that process was not included in the end and I am very pleased that the Hon. Member for Kitchener (Mr. Reimer) has come forward through his motion in an attempt to correct the situation.
The motion before us would add the enjoyment of property to Section 7 of the Charter, thereby guaranteeing the right not
to be deprived of the enjoyment of property, except in accordance with the principles of fundamental justice. In conjunction with that, it is reasonable, I believe, to say that what we are talking about is the unreasonable deprivation of an individual when it comes to property rights.
I suggest that some of the fears I have heard enumerated in the House, that people's rights will be trampled on by the rights of Governments to conduct the business of either the province or the federal Government, are really misplaced. I do not think that is what we are talking about at all. We want to strike a reasonable balance between the property rights of the individual and the legitimate concerns of the state. I would not feel so strongly about this if I had not seen examples in Canadian history where property rights of the individual had been trampled upon.
The House will be aware of all the problems surrounding the expropriation of land for Mirabel Airport. The facts are this: Much more land than necessary was expropriated for the airport. Everybody knew it and acknowledged it. The people whose farms and homes were expropriated fought the issue for years, indeed decades, to do something about it.
I became a believer in this resolution just on that issue alone because I always thought that if property rights had been enshrined in the Constitution, people would have had a legal access and would have been able to take a legal route to show and demonstrate to a court of law that their rights had been unnecessarily deprived. It was a very moving moment for all of us when the then Minister of Public Works spoke to all the farmers who had been deprived of their property and acknowledged that a terrible mistake had been made. All the suffering during those years by those individuals was proved unnecessary.
There is no question that if this motion had been passed and been part of the Constitution, concerned individuals would have had remedy in law. I think that is what we all want. Therefore, I ask all Members to begin the process of enshrining property rights in the Constitution. It is a long and difficult process and I know it will need the support of the provinces. It is long overdue and we should begin the process now.
