Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to have the opportunity to speak in support of the motion introduced by my colleague, the Hon. Member for Kitchener (Mr. Reimer), to amend the Constitution of Canada in order that Section 7 of the Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms reads as follows:
7. Everyone has the right to life, liberty, security of the person and enjoyment of property, and the right not to be deprived thereof except in accordance with the principles of fundamental justice.
The Hon. Member for Kitchener has rightly pointed out that the addition of the words "the enjoyment of property" to Section 7 of the Charter of Rights is a natural adjunct, a given, to those principles that we as Canadians hold dear.
However, the Hon. Member for Cape Breton-The Sydneys (Mr. MacLellan) is on record as saying that "Canadians should not be concerned in any way about the fact that property rights are not enshrined in the Charter of Rights and Freedoms". Yet in a Gallup poll commissioned by the Canadian Real Estate Association 81 per cent of Canadians said "yes", Canadians do feel that it is "fairly" or "very" important
to amend the Constitution in order that property rights be protected.
The right to enjoy property was left out of Section 7 of the Charter of Rights when it was proclaimed in 1982. As a result, Governments are able to pass legislation or make regulations that may violate property rights. The exclusion of property rights is a grave oversight, in my opinion.
Protected property rights go back to 1215 with the signing of the Magna Carta. The right to own is similarly recognized in the English Bill of Rights in 1627, in the United Nations Universal Declaration of Rights which Canada signed in 1948, and finally in the 1960 Canadian Bill of Rights. But now in 1988 we do not have that protection.
The entrenchment of property rights is recognized in many democratic countries, such as the United States, Australia, Italy, Finland, Sweden, and West Germany. In Canada, however, it is not.
The simple acknowledgement of the principle of property rights and the understanding that there is an inherent belief that what one owns or possesses is his right to keep, is a tremendously reassuring principle that has evolved through time. We take a degree of satisfaction and pleasure, perhaps even refuge in our possessions, our reward for hard work.
I take pleasure in sitting in the backyard, working in the flower bed, mowing the lawn, or just puttering around because it affords me a certain degree of peace of mind, contentment, and enjoyment.
But what if my little Shangri-La were taken away from me, for some reason or another? What if my property rights were not recognized? This very real event has happened to many Canadians. Many Canadians were persecuted in their mother country because of government upheavals, changing ideologies, war, or religious persecution. Not only were their human rights violated, but as I argued earlier, property rights, being a direct adjunct, were violated without any form of compensation.
While it is not likely that this occurrence will happen in Canada, the entrenchment of property rights in the Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms would prove to be a safeguard, guaranteeing the rights of property owners against abusive or threatening measures taken against them.
I fully appreciate the difficulties that Hon. Members are encountering in defining the term "property". I believe that all Members from all sides of the House have stated that property encompasses not only property as in real estate, but intellectual property, passive property, and government largesse, which includes welfare payments, old age benefits, unemployment insurance compensation, and so on.
I am in agreement with the Hon. Member for Kitchener who argued that, although it may be difficult to define and interpret "enjoyment of property", it should not detract from the central principle of recognizing and entrenching property rights in the Charter.
February 1, 1988

During the last election campaign, the Progressive Conservative Party took the position that it supported the entrenchment of property rights in the Charter. Since that time, as a result of the Meech Lake Accord, the Province of Quebec has become a constitutional member. Provincial authorities are presently investigating their concerns in regard to property rights.
1 believe that we will do an injustice to the Canadian people if the House does not support the motion presented by the Hon. Member for Kitchener. It is an injustice because the entrenchment of property rights in our Charter is clearly what Canadians want, and it is fundamentally the correct course of action for us to take as parliamentarians.

We are not anywhere near to having an agreement that would actually reduce the emissions that cause acid rain. In the United States, emissions come largely from the midwest. We need emission reduction in the United States parallel to what Canada has done.
Ontario and Quebec have done a remarkable job at reducing sulphur dioxide emissions. We have an understanding that they will be reduced by 50 per cent by 1994. We would very much want to see the Americans making a similar commitment, and I regret to say that we do not have that. 1 do not see that the federal Government is working strenuously to that end, yet every day we hear new news about the effects of acid rain. Today the Presbyterian Church in Hamilton, on James South, is nearly falling down as a result of acid rain. Damage to monuments and buildings is part of the bill which must be paid on acid rain.
[ Translation]
The withering of the maple groves, especially in Quebec, is another problem. The Union des producteurs agricoles taxes Ottawa of weaknesses and spinelessness in the face of the serious problems caused by acid rain from the United States.
An international forum on acid rain will be held soon in Quebec. Experts from the United States and from Europe will be attending. The Quebec provincial Government will be represented, the environmentalists will be there, but not the federal Government.
Now, the withering of the maple groves is caused by the acid rain, especially from the United States. And the European expertise may be usefull to us in Canada, since the withering of European forests is well advanced and the remedies are also well advanced over there.

I regret that the Canadian Government is not going to be there, nor will it provide financial aid for this important conference which is coming up shortly.
The Minister of the Environment (Mr. McMillan) has called acid rain the litmus test regarding the competence of the Government in dealing with environmental questions with the

February 1, 1988
Adjournment debate
United States. I regret to say that that litmus test has been failed. We have a Government which has been actively pursuing a free trade agreement with the Americans. All the while that this has been going on, acid rain has been relegated to a question of lesser importance. In order to get that free trade agreement, that Mulroney-Reagan trade deal, acid rain has been neglected.
I say this with great regret and knowing that the Government has in principle endorsed the Brundtland report, the World Commission on the Environment and Development, which indicates that all economic decisions should have an environmental component. Here we have the major decision for the economy which Canada is facing with the trade deal and the environment was not even considered. The effects of acid rain, the effects of toxic wastes, and the effects of any number of environmental questions, were totally ignored by this Government concerned to move ahead on a trade deal for the wrong reasons.
President Reagan said while he was in Canada that he would consider an agreement with Canada. We have negotiations going on, but they have not been successful. So far the Americans are not willing to specify any actual reductions or specify any timetable. This is essential.
Let us talk about money. Supposedly $5 billion is committed in the United States. Only half of that or $2.5 billion would come from the Government. The rest would come from industry sources. Of that $2.5 billion, $300 million had already been committed to research on acid rain. The Government's commitment, far from being $5 billion, is down to $2.2 billion which in fact has not been appropriated by Congress.
Why not? Our friends in Congress do not see the point in putting more money into research, especially research which will not necessarily reduce the causes of acid rain. Unless we have a real plan with a timetable and with actual remission reductions specified, we are not going to get anywhere.
We need to have two million tonnes of emission reductions from certain areas to improve the situation in Canada. That means 10 million tonnes over all to get the qualitative reductions we need. We are far from it.
Let me close by saying that I think it is absolutely essential that the Government begin to take seriously Canada's number one environmental question, acid rain, and give it a high priority. The first thing it must do is call off the negotiations. We have to send a message to Congress and the administration saying that this kind of negotiation that is going nowhere is not acceptable. Let us begin to prepare the way for a new Congress and a new President. Let us show them that we take the problem very seriously indeed. Let us work on the things that we can work on here at home, especially the effects on human health which we can share with the Americans. Let us not continue this farce of believing that the negotiations we are having with the Americans now will do any good. They will not. Let us look to the future.

speakeroldname: Mrs. Pauline Browes (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of the Environment):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of the Environment
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, 1 am pleased to respond tonight to the Hon. Member's question on the negotiations of the Canada-U.S. acid rain Accord, an issue that is of concern to all Hon. Members. I am pleased that the Hon. Member for Broadview-Greenwood (Ms. McDonald) continues to have this interest.
As you know, Mr. Speaker, Canada has established an acid rain abatement program that will reduce its acid rain emissions to 50 per cent of 1980 levels by 1994. Six of the seven federal-provincial agreements required to fully implement the Canadian program are now in place. The federal Government expects to sign the agreement with Nova Scotia very soon. However, since approximately 50 per cent of the acid rain in eastern Canada originates in the United States, without similar action on the part of our American neighbours, our abatement program cannot be effective in protecting Canada's environment.
Last April, President Reagan agreed to consider Canada's proposal to negotiate a bilateral agreement including targets and schedules to reduce the U.S. trans-boundary flow of acid rain emissions to acceptable levels. Our officials subsequently provided their American counterparts with an outline of the elements Canada feels are essential in an effective Accord.
Publicly, we have stated that we want the U.S. transboundary flow of S02 into eastern Canada to be reduced to two million tonnes by 1994, equivalent to the percentage reduction targets in our own abatement program. This proposal is based on sound scientific information and on existing principles and obligations under international law which provide that countries must ensure that activities within their jurisdictions do not damage the environment of other nations.
Canadian officials met with American counterparts in Ottawa last November 30 but the Americans were not prepared to provide Canada with a formal response to its concept paper at that time. The American negotiating team stated that a decision regarding the American position would be made by the President's domestic policy council at its mid-January meeting and that they would provide Canada with a substantive response to the proposal on January 25.
The Minister of the Environment (Mr. McMillan) has indicated that the American response received in Washington on January 25 was sorely inadequate. The main components of an Accord which the Americans were prepared to negotiate with Canada include: one, a heavy emphasis on joint research, emission monitoring and further problem definition; two, recognition by Canada that market-force-driven implementation of new technologies and deregulation will significantly reduce future U.S. emissions; and three, the most disturbing element for Canada, the position that any Accord could not include scientific emission targets and schedules.
February 1, 1988

This counterproposal indeed falls far short of the key elements needed to protect Canada's environment. As the Minister of the Environment stated in the House on January 26, he, the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Clark) and the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) are currently reviewing every available option that will enable Canada to obtain the reduction it requires in the U.S. trans-boundary flow of acid rain. A decision on how the Government intends to proceed will be announced shortly, but Hon. Members may rest assured that the federal Government will continue to pursue this vital environmental issue with the United States, with the administration, with the Congress and with the American public.
GOVERNMENT APPOINTMENTS-REQUEST FOR COMMITTEE SCRUTINY/REQUEST FOR NATIVE REPRESENTATION ON BOARD

Mr. Speaker, my appearance on the Adjournment Debate this evening arises from the unsatisfactory answers given by the Minister of Regional Industrial Expansion and Minister of State for Science and Technology (Mr. de Cotret) on November 23, 1987. He was responding to my question concerning the composition and representation of membership of the board of the FEDNOR agency, as the acronym has it, or the Advisory Committee on Development for Northern Ontario, as 1 believe the official title is. I asked the Minister if the Government would be appointing more members to the board. Having initially said there were seven more vacancies, in his reply to my supplementary question he said:
There are 12 members on the board. There are still four vacancies to be
filled.
That was well over two months ago and those vacancies have not yet been filled. I believe the Parliamentary Secretary should account for that omission.
I would like to point out that three nights ago the Standing Committee on Regional Industrial Expansion had the eight present nominees to the board come before it for their confirmation hearings. It rapidly became evident, under very probing and perceptive questioning by the Hon. Member for Nickel Belt (Mr. Rodriguez), that seven of the appointees owed their appointments to their connections with the Progressive Conservative Party. That is really not the gravamen of my complaint in this matter. We expect the Government to appoint Tories to the board. This certainly is not going to be one of the most financially lucrative boards to which a supporter of the Government could possibly aspire. I might say incidentally that the eighth appointee appeared to be a partisan of the Liberal Party. Indeed, one of the seven left some doubt as to where his current loyalties lay, although it was clear as to how his appointment was arranged.
Those four vacancies have to be used to get some balance on the board. I am sure that the Hon. Parliamentary Secretary is not going to tell me that a board made up completely or almost completely of people who have a firm allegiance to the
Adjournment debate
Progressive Conservative Party is going to be a board that will be capable of rendering fully objective decisions no matter how strong their background in business, how strong their understanding of regional development, or how strong their understanding of financing programs might be.
It was obvious from those who came before us on I believe it was Thursday night that the native element of northern Ontario, a very significant element numerically and even more so if we consider the lack of employment and underdevelopment of the 100 odd reserves in northern Ontario, was not represented on this board. Yet the chairman of the board acknowledge with some pride, I am glad to say, that the board would be having an active interaction, an active role, in regard to the economic development of native communities. If that be so, and I trust it is, there should be representation that reflects and is conversant with the realities of the economic situation of native communities.
Another obvious component that was not represented among the eight who appeared before us was that of labour. Organized labour is very strong in northern Ontario with its resource industries of mining and forestry in particular. Organized labour of course has many representatives who have very well-developed ideas on the nature of regional development, on regional development needs, and could contribute a great deal to this board.
Finally, I think it is proper to point out that the resource and processing industries, which are the raison d'etre, if you like, for the economy of northern Ontario in very large measure, were significantly under-represented on this board. Indeed, the board members collectively could only claim, I would say, a passing familiarity with resource industries.
Mining, the forest industry, and the forest resource processing industries such as sawmills and pulp and paper mills need to be represented on this board if we are to have a balanced composition.
I was glad to see that the matter of potential conflict of interest has been taken care of. Let it not be said that I will not compliment the Government when such a compliment is earned.
We did, of course, highlight in our questioning the over-all inadequacy of the funding allowed for the FEDNOR agency. There is $40 million available for grant distribution plus $60 million in loan guarantees. Not to criticize, contrast that with the Atlantic Canada Opportunities Agencies which has something like five times the per capita available funding.
The basic question which I would like to hear the Parliamentary Secretary answer this evening is when appointments will be made to those four open positions and whether they will be made in such a way as to ensure that we end up with a balanced board, not only in terms of ideology but in terms of the community of interest of northern Ontario they represent.

speakeroldname: Mr. J. M. Forrestall (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Regional Industrial Expansion):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of State for Science and Technology; Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Regional Industrial Expansion
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, at the outset I would like to remind the distinguished Member for Kenora- Rainy River (Mr. Parry) that ACOA deals with four provinces while FEDNOR deals with northern Ontario.
Were the Minister here this evening, I am sure he would welcome the opportunity to bring to the attention of Members in the Chamber again the very important and very major thrusts which the Government is making toward the economic rehabilitation of northern Ontario. As you know, Mr. Speaker, FEDNOR is the recently announced federal economic development initiative for northern Ontario. A key component is a $55 million fund, and there are different ways to explain the levels of the funding. Its intention is to fill the gaps which exist in federal programming with respect to that region. I think that is particularly fair to say with regard to new native economic thrust for the future.
The Northern Ontario Development Advisory Board was established to provide an important source of advice to the Government on federal economic policies, programs, and services, particularly as they relate to FEDNOR and economic redevelopment.
The eight board members, announced on October 9 last by the Member for Sault Ste. Marie (Mr. Kelleher), the Hon. Solicitor General, on behalf of the Minister for Regional Industrial Expansion (Mr. de Cotret), are all northerners and represent the region's geographic districts. They bring with them a wide variety of expertise and experience together with
a very deep and personal commitment to the economic redevelopment of northern Ontario.
There has been some suggestion here this evening that all such nominations by the Governor in Council are subject to the approval of the appropriate committee of the House. These eight, as the Member has just indicated, were all, if I am correct, before the committee only last week.
The Order in Council establishing the board does provide for 12 members and eight of them have been appointed. There are four appointments yet to be made and these vacancies will be filled with the assistance of suggestions coming not only from the Member for Kenora-Rainy River but all those interested in the orderly economic development of that part of Ontario. Suggestions will come from native people, labour, and the resource based industries, which, as the Hon. Member has mentioned, are so important.
Since the announcement last fall the board has been meeting regularly. Planning and discussion of appropriate programs are ongoing. There will be a secretariat established in Sault Ste. Marie. I think the Member will be pleased to join with all of us in applauding this first step. The board will be rounded and fleshed out to its full membership. I know it will do an excellent job for that part of the country.
